title: Efficient construction of subspace design codes over constant alphabet
abstract: Subspace-design codes form a central unifying framework in coding theory, connecting probabilistic existence results and explicit algebraically structured constructions. The two core families are folded Reed-Solomon codes and univariate multiplicity codes, both possessing the subspace-design property. These codes reach list-decoding capacity with polynomial-size lists, but their alphabet size grows with code length and hurts practical efficiency. Goyal, Guruswami, and Hsieh achieved a major breakthrough: they constructed the first explicit subspace-design codes over constant-size alphabets via the Alon-Edmonds-Luby expander framework, settling an open problem and showing subspace-design properties can hold without large alphabets. Despite recent progress, constructing subspace-design codes with low-complexity efficient encoding remains a critical open challenge. This work gives an explicit construction of r-dimensional subspace-design codes over a constant alphabet whose size grows exponentially with r. By comparison, Goyal et al. (FOCS 2026) built r-dimensional subspace-design codes with alphabet size doubly exponential in r squared. Our construction is computationally efficient: encoding scales quadratically with block length and linearly with dimension r in field operations. We use modified algebraic geometry codes, replacing rational evaluation points with higher-degree places to obtain a valid additive code. To confirm parameter bounds, we use Moore matrices to analyze determinants with many zero entries. We also generalize univariate multiplicity codes, originally built from Reed-Solomon codes, to algebraic geometry codes, and prove these AG-multiplicity codes achieve optimal parameters.

title: Bridging the Topological Divide: Dual-Branch Graph Distillation with Semantic Priors for Robust Cold-Start Recommendation
abstract: Graph Collaborative Filtering models have achieved remarkable success in recommendation systems. However, they inherently suffer from a catastrophic representation collapse in strict cold-start scenarios due to the topological isolation of unobserved items. While integrating multi-modal semantic features offers a potential remedy, directly mapping isolated semantic attributes into a globally topology-driven collaborative space frequently precipitates representation degradation and optimization conflicts. To bridge this fundamental structural divide, we propose DualGCN, an innovative Dual-Branch Graph Knowledge Distillation Framework. Operating under a decoupled two-stage training paradigm, DualGCN first constructs a robust collaborative teacher network where item representations are anchored by a topology-smoothed semantic prior, effectively reshaping the latent manifold. Subsequently, a semantic student branch employs a residual mapping mechanism and a magnitude-agnostic cosine distillation objective to achieve high-fidelity cross-modal alignment without disrupting established collaborative signals. Furthermore, we introduce a dynamic norm reconstruction mechanism to rigorously calibrate the physical scales of novel and warm items during global retrieval. Extensive experiments across three real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that DualGCN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in strict cold-start scenarios while comprehensively preserving recommendation accuracy for highly active items.

title: Retrieving Metrological Information from Noisy Squeezed Spin States via Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Frequency inhomogeneity can obscure the metrological advantage of squeezed spin states, making the choice of readout crucial. We study interacting spin-1/2 ensembles with static local frequency disorder and optimize a common collective readout over independent disorder realizations. Using Bayesian optimization of the full measurement-outcome distribution, we identify observables combining dipole and quadrupole operators that yield greater classical Fisher information than the optimized dipole readout considered here. For ensembles of up to 17 spins, their disorder-averaged CFI surpasses the standard quantum limit at both disorder strengths studied, including a regime where the dipole readout remains below it. For the larger ensembles studied, fixing the encoding axis to the direction that maximizes the disorder-averaged quantum Fisher information retains nearly the same performance. These results identify a route to extracting metrological information from frequency-disordered spin ensembles through the choice of collective observable.

title: Communication Strategies for Cognitive Radar Networks
abstract: Distributed radar networks provide the ability to monitor large and dynamic scenes by uti- lizing multiple spatially separated sensors. However, the effectiveness of such networks are constrained by limited communication resources if a central fusion center needs to collect raw data from all the radar nodes. This thesis investigates adaptive radar resource manage- ment for multi-radar multi-target tracking through the application of multi-armed bandit based scheduling methods. A simulated radar network is developed where multiple radars observe maneuvering targets while providing track updates to a centralized fusion center. Several radar selection strategies based on ϵ-Greedy and Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) multi-armed bandits are investigated and compared against a baseline communication strat- egy. Radar selection is performed by utilizing contextual information at the fusion center derived from the current tracking state and spatial distribution of targets, which allows communication resources to be dedicated to radars of interest. The performance of the re- sulting developed tracking system is evaluated using the Generalized Optimal Sub-Pattern Assignment (GOSPA) metric. Simulation results demonstrate that the adaptive scheduling methods improve tracking performance by concentrating resources on regions of high target density, while the relative results between communication methods depends highly on target conditions and communication constraints.

title: ReviewIQ: AI-Based Product Review Intelligence and Consumer Insight System Using NLP, Deep Learning, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: This research paper proposes an AI Co-Founder system designed to support early-stage entrepreneurs in making informed business decisions. The system uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), persistent company memory, semantic search, and external competitor intelligence to provide context-aware recommendations. It introduces Persistent Entrepreneurial Decision Intelligence (PEDI), an approach that combines startup information, historical context, and market evidence to help founders identify risks, opportunities, and information gaps. The paper presents the architecture and prototype implementation, discusses its limitations, and outlines future research directions for AI-driven entrepreneurial decision support.

title: Memory Economics in Generational Artificial Life: How Environmental Volatility Dictates the Phase Boundary Between Lamarckian Inheritance and Agile Amnesia
abstract: In evolutionary computation, cultural evolution, and continual machine learning, lineages face a fundamental tension between retaining ancestral knowledge (stability) and acquiring novel skills (plasticity). While exact "Lamarckian" parameter transfer accelerates adaptation in static environments, real biological and cultural lineages operate under strict metabolic budgets and non-stationary conditions. In this unified treatise, we formalize the theory of Memory Economics: 1. The Capacity-Saturation Trap: When agent memory capacity is strictly bounded, exact cloning causes catastrophic failure under environmental volatility (p < 10^-5), establishing lossy transmission as an indispensable mathematical regularizer. 2. Memory Economics Phase Diagram: By allowing retention (f), learning rate (lr), and memory capacity (c) to co-evolve under metabolic costs, we map a distinct non-monotonic phase diagram across shift timescales (N=30 independent runs per regime, Welch's t = 30.925, p = 2.86e-32, Cohen's d = 7.98, SHA-256 verified). Rapid volatility produces a "boomerang" strategy; intermediate volatility forces "agile amnesia" where 85.6% of active memory is newly learned; stable eras foster "Lamarckian rentiers." 3. Neural Continual Learning: We demonstrate that this phase boundary translates directly to deep neural network agents (MLPs) undergoing continual classification on non-stationary, alternating task boundaries.

title: Two-Stage Score Estimation for Group-Specific Diffusion Models
abstract: Generative modeling across related distributions raises a question: how can shared structure support accurate generation for a target distribution with limited observations? We develop a statistical framework for diffusion transfer that analyzes a shared pooled score together with a target-specific offset. Under Besov regularity of the pooled density and a stable hierarchical composition model for the offset, we derive convergence rates that separate the costs of learning these components and identify when a simpler offset yields a faster risk-bound rate than separate fitting. Under suitable boundary and regularity assumptions, we prove that the offset remains bounded and jointly regular as diffusion time approaches zero. These results allow the lower time cutoff to vanish polynomially and provide total-variation guarantees for diffusion models as density estimators. Synthetic simulations and image benchmarks provide a proof of concept for the framework.

title: Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation
abstract: Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yufanchen96/RPD

title: E2DRL: End-to-End Differentiable Reinforcement Learning for 3D Obstacle Avoidance in Quadruped Robots
abstract: Differentiable reinforcement learning shows strong promise for robot policy learning, but its application to legged locomotion has remained limited to blind walking or simulated 2D tasks. Extending it to end-to-end visual obstacle avoidance is challenging because hard collision constraints and early termination upon contact corrupt first-order gradients, trapping optimizers in local minima. We present E2DRL, which addresses this with a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation: penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping to provide the first-order training signals for 3D obstacle avoidance. To realize a deployable perception-control system, a privileged teacher trained via Soft Analytic Policy Optimization (SAPO) in a differentiable simulator is distilled into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, then blended with a base locomotion policy using a terrain-aware gating module for deployment. In simulation, E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO and demonstrates superior velocity-tracking performance and 3D obstacle-avoidance capability compared with both PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC. We present the first sim-to-real validation of end-to-end differentiable RL for 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.

title: Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Memory Management, Coordination Failures and Semantic Conflict Resolution
abstract: As large language model (LLM) systems move from using one agent at a time to working with multiple agents together, keeping the system stable and ensuring memory stays accurate is still a major challenge. Making linear tasks work with multiple agents hurts performance by up to 70% because of extra communication and problems that spread out, but tasks that can be done at the same time can improve performance by up to 81% (Kim et al., 2025). Right now, the memory management tools we use like flat conversation logs, RAG retrieval and single-agent versioning systems (Wu et al., 2025; Su et al., 2026) do not work well when there are conflicts in open-domain semantic merges. They either need strict locks or special compilers for specific domains to handle these issues. To tackle these bottlenecks, this review paper brings together real-world failure categories, system-level checks and memory designs. It introduces a Git-managed multi-agent framework that includes dynamic task assignment, secure branch execution in isolated environments and external oversight using an LLM as a judge, along with council-based meaning-based decision making. In the end, we identify and outline the main research questions that still need to be addressed in areas like sharing experiences between different agents, figuring out the causes of faults and resolving conflicts in meaning.

title: Parallel-World Self-Supervision with Adaptive Switching Between Self-Supervision and Collaborative Supervision in Large Language Models
abstract: Self-supervised learning provides a foundation for learning from unlabeled data, while collaborative supervision enables multiple models or agents to exchange information and improve the quality of learning signals. However, relying exclusively on self-supervision may reinforce a model's existing errors, whereas continuous collaborative supervision may introduce unnecessary computational costs, correlated errors, and conflicting learning signals. This paper proposes Parallel-World Self-Supervision with Adaptive Switching between Self-Supervision and Collaborative Supervision (PWSC-Supervision), a unified framework for large language models (LLMs). The framework constructs multiple parallel worlds from a shared base model, with each world pursuing a distinct supervision orientation, learning objective, or evaluation perspective. Each world can independently generate, examine, and refine its own supervision signals. An adaptive controller determines whether a given learning instance should be handled through self-supervision, collaboration among parallel worlds, or collaboration with heterogeneous external models. The controller considers uncertainty, disagreement, estimated supervision quality, task difficulty, computational cost, and historical learning performance. Supervision signals are filtered and weighted according to their reliability before being used for model adaptation. The framework further supports dynamic changes in collaboration topology, supervision direction, and model participation. We formulate the learning process as a constrained optimization problem and present an implementable algorithm and an experimental evaluation protocol. The proposed framework aims to provide a systematic approach to balancing autonomous learning and collaborative learning rather than imposing a single supervision strategy on every task. Its effectiveness, computational efficiency, and generalization capabilities remain empirical questions to be investigated.

title: Adaptive Reasoning and Collaborative Reasoning Switching Across Parallel Worlds of Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve complex problem-solving through deliberate reasoning, multiple reasoning trajectories, self-evaluation, and collaboration among agents. However, existing approaches often emphasize one dominant reasoning configuration, such as independent reasoning, parallel sampling, iterative self-refinement, or multi-agent collaboration. These configurations may be inefficient when task difficulty, uncertainty, reasoning progress, and computational constraints vary dynamically. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Reasoning and Collaboration (APW-RC), a conceptual framework in which multiple reasoning worlds are instantiated from the same underlying LLM or from heterogeneous LLMs. Each parallel world explores a distinct reasoning direction and independently adapts its reasoning strategy according to local evidence, uncertainty, progress, and resource constraints. A coordination controller dynamically determines whether a world should continue independent adaptive reasoning, collaborate with other worlds, or request assistance from external models. Collaboration can occur between worlds instantiated from the same model, between heterogeneous models, or across both groups. The framework combines trajectory diversity, local adaptation, selective information exchange, cross-model assistance, and cost-aware switching within a unified inference-time architecture. We formulate the switching problem as sequential decision-making under computational constraints and introduce a proposed objective that balances solution quality, reliability, diversity, latency, and computational expenditure. We also describe an implementation procedure, evaluation protocol, baseline systems, ablation studies, and potential failure modes. The framework is a research proposal rather than an experimentally validated system. Its principal research question is whether adaptive switching between independent reasoning and collaborative reasoning across parallel worlds can improve the quality–cost trade-off compared with fixed-mode reasoning and conventional multi-agent collaboration.

title: Aspect Term Extraction and Hierarchical Kronecker Deep Learning Network for Sentiment Classification
abstract: The process of natural language processing (NLP) to classify and identify sentiments as negative, positive, or neutral automatically is called sentiment classification. Sentiment Analysis improves the service and product based on customer feedback. Sentiment Analysis is beneficial for business operations for analyzing customer feedback to improve customer satisfaction and product development. However, there are some limitations, such as overfitting issues, flexibility, interpretability, generalization, stability, low energy efficiency, and complexity. The traditional methods do not capture the contextual semantics of the sentence, which leads to poor sentiment classification in the presence of sarcasm, irony, or idiomatic expressions. Also, many of the methods ignore the textural cues like hashtags, all-caps words, punctuation, and negations. To overcome above-mentioned issues, an efficient hierarchical Kronecker deep learning network (HKDL-Net) is established. Here, HKDL-Net is developed by the combination of hierarchical deep learning for text classification (HDLTex) and deep Kronecker network (DKN). Initially, reviews are subjected to bidirectional encoder representation from transformers (BERT) tokenization to split text into specific words. Then, aspect term extraction (ATE) is performed. Afterwards, feature extraction is executed by using extracted aspect terms for mining features, such as emotion, hashtag, all-caps, number of sentences in review, elongated units, numerical words, a bag of units, question marks, number of words in a review, and negation. The sentiment classification is ultimately achieved through the proposed HKDL-Net. Moreover, HKDL-Net attained better results in sentiment classification with a precision of 91.877%, recall of 93.899%, F1-score of 92.877%, and accuracy of 97.568%, respectively. This shows that the devised model effectively detects the non-standard language and enhances the classification performance of sentiments in subtle or complex cases. Also, it can capture contextual relationships between words, which helps to improve its ability to understand sarcasm, irony, or idiomatic expressions.

title: Serial H&E Pathology Reveals Progression‐Associated Nuclear Size Drift as a Longitudinal Digital Readout of Bladder Cancer Evolution
abstract: Serial pathological specimens are routinely generated during bladder cancer surveillance, but their temporal information remains underused in computational pathology. This study develops a longitudinal digital pathology framework to quantify direction-preserving nuclear morphological change within the same patient. Paired hematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images are organized as T0, the earlier specimen, and T1, the later specimen. Signed Δ features, defined as T1-T0, are extracted across nuclear size, shape regularity, local cellularity, and spatial organization. After quality control, the discovery cohort includes 86 pairs from 86 patients, and the independent confirmation cohort includes 96 pairs from 96 patients. A separate four-center resource of 1977 whole-slide images from 1660 patients provides a static contextual baseline. Several nuclear features showed the same direction of association with progression across the two cohorts. Nuclear size-related change was most prominent in the independent confirmation cohort, particularly for equivalent nuclear diameter and nuclear area. Spatial analysis shows a broader upward distributional shift in nuclear area in progression pairs. Static foundation-model representations show variable locked cross-center transferability, whereas Ki-67 immunohistochemistry and TCGA-BLCA transcriptomic analyses provide complementary tissue-level and molecular context. Routine serial hematoxylin and eosin specimens may therefore provide interpretable, direction-preserving digital readouts of bladder cancer evolution.

title: Feed-Forward Multi-View Feature Coding for 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods enable efficient reconstruction of 3D scenes from sparse multi-view images in a single forward pass, without scene-specific optimization. However, existing feed-forward scene-coding pipelines first generate a complete Gaussian representation and then encode its geometry and appearance attributes separately, often involving non-differentiable operations. The resulting 'generate-then-compress' pipeline requires complex attribute-specific codec designs and limits rate-distortion performance by restricting the exploitation of cross-attribute redundancy. We propose multi-view feature coding for Gaussian splatting (MFGS), an end-to-end feed-forward framework for scene coding. Instead of compressing an explicit Gaussian representation, MFGS extracts multi-view features from the input images and encodes them into a compact bitstream. Through end-to-end rate-distortion training, MFGS learns compact multi-view features that jointly represent geometry and appearance, enabling the receiver to predict Gaussian attributes from the decoded features. We further introduce importance-guided Gaussian selection to accommodate different rendering budgets, allowing the receiver to adjust the number of Gaussians used for rendering from the same bitstream. Across RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV, MFGS achieves 99.76-99.86% bitrate savings over the generate-then-compress pipeline, as measured by BD-rate, while reducing total GMACs by 52-55% and providing an approximately 12 times end-to-end speedup.

title: Geometric-resource bounds and permutation-averaged success probabilities for the WZP algorithm
abstract: Solving linear systems of equations is a fundamental task in machine learning and optimization. In this work, we extend the original WZP algorithm from real symmetric linear systems to complex Hermitian linear systems. We then study the success probability of the modified WZP algorithm from a resource-theoretic perspective. By expressing the postselection success probability as the expectation value of a positive operator, we derive upper and lower bounds of the maximal success probability over separable, incoherent, and real pure states. These bounds further establish connections between the maximal success probability and geometric entanglement, coherence, and imaginarity. We further show that, under permutation averaging, the averaged success probability is an affine function of the coherence fraction, with its dependence determined by the alignment between the success operator and the equal-superposition state. We also investigate the preprocessed WZP algorithm under subgroup-constrained preprocessing. For the two-level family, the optimal success probability is determined by the maximal projection weight onto the orbit of the target projector. Our results provide a unified perspective on the WZP success probability under different operational constraints.

title: Bilinear Compressive Security with Finitely Many Samples
abstract: Bilinear Compressive Security (BCS) is a lightweight encryption scheme that combines compressed sensing with a fresh random convolution filter to improve resistance against key-recovery attacks under key reuse. Previous work derived information-theoretic guarantees for BCS by relating key identifiability to phase retrieval under the assumption that an adversary has access to the full ciphertext distribution induced by the random filter. In practice, however, an adversary only observes finitely many encryptions, leaving the security of BCS in the finite-sample regime largely unexplored. In this paper, we study key recovery from only finitely many observations. We first develop a covariance-based attack that estimates the linear measurements from repeated encryptions of the same plaintext and subsequently recovers the secret measurement matrix. We analyze the estimation procedure and derive finite-sample guarantees together with corresponding sample-complexity bounds. We further investigate the complete attack experimentally and compare its observed recovery behavior with the previously established information-theoretic identifiability results. Our experiments show two qualitatively different recovery regimes on the structure of the measurement matrix. For dense matrices, including Gaussian matrices, the number of measurements required for successful recovery appears to grow linearly with the signal dimension. This differs from the worst-case behavior suggested by information theory. In contrast, for matrices with sparse rows, we observe a quadratic growth consistent with the theoretical bound. These results suggest that the sparsity structure of the measurement matrix plays an important role in the security of BCS and should be taken into account when selecting parameters and designing practical instances of the scheme.

title: One Agent per Zone: Decentralised Active Inference under Partial Observability for Multi-Zone HVAC Control on Edge Hardware
abstract: Multi-zone HVAC control is a shared-resource problem: zones on a floor share one fan and cooling coil, so each zone's demand affects its neighbours and the building's peak power. One controller per zone scales well and isolates faults, but each controller then observes only its own zone, not the shared air loop. In this work, we present a decentralised controller that assigns each zone an independent active-inference agent, which plans by minimising expected free energy and learns its zone dynamics online. The agents exchange no messages, so none depends on peers or a coordinator; each accounts for the unobserved coupling through a latent disturbance and a congestion signal derived from the metered power of the other floors. Fifteen agents are evaluated in EnergyPlus on a Sinergym office building against three rule-based controllers and three MADDPG fleets, one given the same floor meters. On five noisy weather years unseen during training, the fleet attains the lowest mean building peak (88.3 kW, 3 to 17 % below the baselines) and staggers the floor peaks better than any baseline, with a coincidence factor (building peak over the sum of the floor peaks) of 0.929 versus 0.936 to 0.994. Compared with a reactive rule at similar comfort (0.912 versus 0.916), it lowers the sum of monthly peaks, on which demand charges are billed, by 33 kW (4 %) in every year, at the cost of about 10 % more energy. It costs 9% less per year than the proactive rule (at lower comfort) and 1% less than the MADDPG fleet given the same floor meters, in every test year. The whole fleet runs on a single low-cost Raspberry Pi 5, closing the observation-to-action loop over MQTT in 442 ms at p95, far below the 15-minute control step.

title: Data Curation and Model Souping: Unlocking Qwen3-0.6B for MS MARCO Passage Ranking
abstract: This report studies passage retrieval and re-ranking on the MS MARCO benchmark using lightweight Qwen3-0.6B models. Across three experimental settings --- BM25-then-reranking task, corpus-wide dense retrieval task, and dense retrieval then re-ranking task --- the results demonstrate that competitive ranking performance can be achieved without complex architectural modifications, custom loss functions, or cross-encoder distillation. Instead, substantial gains stem from data-centric strategies: corpus-targeted continued pre-training, rigorous data curation, hard-negative mining, training--inference distribution alignment, and weight merging via Model Soup. In particular, Model Soup delivers marked performance gains while preserving the inference efficiency of a single model. These findings highlight how data curation and weight merging can push sub-billion-parameter models to state-of-the-art performance. My models can be downloaded from Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/shuguangh/models

title: Defenses contra prompt injection en agents LLM: avaluació sistemàtica i anàlisi mecanicista de modes de fallada
abstract: [EN] Agents based on large language models (LLMs) with access to external tools have become the standard architecture for production artificial intelligence systems. Their exposure to external content makes them vulnerable to prompt injection: the insertion of malicious instructions into data that the agent processes. This exposure has been identified by the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) as the main security risk for LLM applications. Although recent literature proposes numerous defenses, these methods are evaluated under heterogeneous conditions that prevent rigorous comparison. This Master's Thesis addresses this gap through a systematic and reproducible evaluation of eight representative state-of-the-art defenses (Spotlighting, StruQ, SecAlign, PromptGuard, paraphrasing, sandwich, reminder and baseline), which are applied to models covering both commercial and open-source systems of different sizes. The experimental protocol is built on the AgentDojo and InjecAgent benchmarks, applying utility, robustness and refusal metrics in the evaluation, supported by statistical tests. The work is complemented by a mechanistic interpretability study, which applies techniques such as activation patching and logit lens, in order to characterize which internal components of the model are causally responsible for the failure of the defenses.

title: Adaptive Autonomous and Collaborative Exploration in Parallel Worlds of Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Exploration Mode Switching
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can explore solution spaces independently, generate alternative hypotheses, investigate unfamiliar directions, and collaborate with other agents. However, autonomous exploration and collaborative exploration are often implemented as separate procedures or combined through predefined interaction protocols. Such designs may limit the ability of an agent system to determine when independent exploration is preferable and when information exchange or coordinated exploration is more beneficial. This paper proposes Adaptive Autonomous and Collaborative Exploration in Parallel Worlds (AACE-PW), a conceptual framework that integrates parallel exploration instances of the same underlying LLM with heterogeneous external LLMs through adaptive exploration-mode switching. Each parallel world operates under a distinct exploration direction, hypothesis, objective, or strategy while retaining the underlying model identity. Worlds can explore independently, exchange selected discoveries, jointly investigate promising directions, or return to independent exploration when collaboration becomes redundant or restrictive. External LLMs can contribute different architectures, capabilities, tools, and reasoning strategies. A supervisory controller evaluates uncertainty, novelty, diversity, progress, agreement, information gain, communication cost, and computational budget to select among autonomous, intra-model collaborative, cross-model collaborative, and hybrid exploration modes. The framework distinguishes parallel inference instances from independent model training and specifies an implementable control policy, an evaluation protocol, and testable hypotheses. Its potential contributions include preserving exploratory diversity, reducing premature convergence, improving resource allocation, and supporting dynamic coordination across heterogeneous model agents. Because the framework is conceptual, its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing adaptive exploration and multi-agent routing methods require empirical validation.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Diagnosis and Mutual Diagnosis for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate complex responses, but their outputs may contain factual errors, logical inconsistencies, unsupported claims, and omissions. Self-diagnosis enables a model to inspect its own outputs, whereas mutual diagnosis enables multiple models to examine one another's outputs. However, relying exclusively on either mode may introduce limitations. Self-diagnosis can preserve the original model's blind spots, while mutual diagnosis can incur additional computational costs and may propagate shared errors or produce unproductive disagreement. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Mutual Diagnosis Switching (ASMD), a framework in which multiple LLMs dynamically select between self-diagnosis and mutual diagnosis according to the observed diagnostic state. The framework incorporates initial response generation, structured error identification, diagnostic confidence estimation, cross-model disagreement analysis, diagnosis-mode selection, feedback-guided revision, and termination control. Rather than requiring a fixed sequence in which every model first diagnoses itself and then consults other models, ASMD treats the choice of diagnosis mode as a sequential decision problem. A lightweight switching policy estimates the expected benefit of additional diagnosis relative to its computational cost and selects an appropriate diagnostic configuration. The framework also includes safeguards against correlated judgments, unsupported corrections, and premature acceptance of consensus. This paper formalizes the architecture, defines the switching policy, presents an implementable algorithm, and proposes an empirical evaluation protocol covering reasoning, factual question answering, mathematical problem solving, and code generation. Because no experiments are conducted in this conceptual study, no performance improvements are claimed as established results. The proposed framework provides a testable approach to investigating whether adaptive coordination between self-diagnosis and mutual diagnosis can improve output reliability and computational efficiency compared with fixed diagnostic strategies.

title: LLM-Driven User Preference Topic Modeling for Design Decision Support
abstract: Online reviews of home medical devices are noisy, heterogeneous, and uneven in information density, which makes it hard to turn the voice of the customer into engineering design decisions. This study proposes and validates a review-mining framework that couples rule-based data governance with a locally deployed large language model (LLM) and complex-network analysis. Taking home oxygen concentrators as the case, we collected 25,893 raw review entries from JD.com, Taobao, and Tmall. Because overlapping collection windows made 80.4% of these rows redundant (5084 unique review texts), a four-stage pipeline combining regular-expression cleaning, domain-relevance filtering, low-value review removal, and exact-plus-prefix deduplication refined them into a 2238-review corpus (44.0% of the unique review texts). A locally hosted Qwen3-8B model then performed aspect-level extraction within nine predefined design aspects, yielding 6068 structured aspect–topic–confidence records from 2214 reviews (98.9% parsing success), and scored sentiment for 6052 unique review–aspect pairs on a [−1, 1] scale. From these records, we built a topic co-occurrence network (202 nodes and 1895 edges after low-frequency filtering) and ranked design requirements with a Composite Centrality Index (CCI; weights 0.4/0.4/0.2 over min–max-normalized degree, betweenness, and closeness). Simple Operation (CCI = 1.000) and Low Noise (0.981) dominate user preference, followed by Solid Build Quality (0.611) and Oxygen Concentration (0.574); sentiment is strongly polarized on acoustic experience (Low Noise +0.755 vs. Excessive Noise −0.560). Five checks support these findings: an LDA baseline produced substantially coarser, partly brand-dominated topics; the CCI ranking is stable under five alternative weightings (Spearman’s ρ ≥ 0.978) and across 16 combinations of network-construction thresholds; bootstrap resampling (B = 1000) places the top two topics within ranks 1–2 with 95% confidence; the leading themes replicate in a JD.com-only subnetwork; and manual validation of a stratified 450-pair sample (two blinded annotators, adjudicated gold standard) gave 87.6% aspect accuracy and 94.4% sentiment-polarity accuracy. The framework converts unstructured reviews into a quantified, traceable design-priority list for oxygen concentrator development; we interpret the resulting associations as descriptive evidence for prioritization, not as causal effects.

title: A two-stage RAG-LLM pipeline for roadmapping neuroscience research in operational environments
abstract: Introduction Neuroscientific research and applications in real world environments are often constrained by limited access, equipment limitations, and high costs. Consequently, robustly selecting constructs to focus effort on is a high-impact task. Method This study introduces a two-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline that generates research roadmaps from existing real-world data to inform research priorities in the field, given the state of the art. Stage 1 uses retrieval-augmented generation on operational logs to identify candidate psychological, social, and neurocognitive constructs and map their co-occurrence. Stage 2 evaluates how well these constructs are represented in the literature across four dimensions that commonly inform prioritization: ecological validity, neural correlates, biosensor protocols, and brain computer interface readiness, producing an evidence gap matrix. Pipeline evaluation combined human review, deterministic computations, and human-LLM alignment analysis. Results Applying the pipeline to Mars Desert Research Station logs, Stage 1 identified 19 constructs. Stage 2 highlighted critical gaps in neuroimaging and measurement protocols, particularly for social domains, thereby identifying potential research priorities and risks. Discussion This methodology offers a generalizable starting point for synthesizing operational logs into actionable research roadmaps, but the evaluation showed it still required human scrutiny.

title: An interpretable machine learning framework for retrospective attribution of hospitalization costs in patients with chronic kidney disease
abstract: Hospitalization costs vary substantially among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet the factors underlying this heterogeneity are not fully understood. We developed an interpretable machine learning framework to retrospectively characterize differences in hospitalization costs among patients with CKD and externally evaluated its performance. The study included 3,017 hospitalizations from one tertiary hospital and 2,708 hospitalizations from another tertiary hospital for external validation. Patients were analyzed separately according to kidney transplant status, including non-transplant ( n = 2,435) and transplant ( n = 582) groups. Multiple machine learning and conventional statistical models were compared using temporal holdout testing, external validation, and sensitivity analyses. LightGBM performed best in the non-transplant group (R² = 0.7060), whereas XGBoost performed best in the transplant group (R² = 0.6235). External validation yielded R² values of 0.5921 and 0.5513, respectively. Model interpretation identified length of stay, treatment-related features, age, and selected laboratory measures as prominent contributors to predicted costs, with nonlinear patterns and substantial patient-level heterogeneity. This framework provides a transparent approach for retrospective hospitalization cost attribution and case-mix analysis in CKD.

title: Single-Shuffle Card-Based Protocols for Any Boolean Circuit with Six Cards per Gate
abstract: Abstract Card-based protocols perform secure computation using physical playing cards, and their efficiency is primarily evaluated by two metrics: the number of cards and the number of shuffles. In this paper, we present three new card-based protocols that reduce the number of cards. The first protocol supports any Boolean circuit and decreases the number of cards. The second protocol extends the first to a committed-format version, while the third is specialized for Boolean circuits without a branched input, achieving an even smaller number of cards. All the proposed protocols are based on Yao’s garbled-circuit framework, similar to previous single-shuffle card-based protocols. Our main contribution is a novel encoding method that represents the truth table of each Boolean gate with fewer cards than existing schemes. Consequently, our protocols require only six cards per gate in a single-shuffle execution, providing a significant improvement in efficiency over prior work. Furthermore, by incorporating the card-based free-XOR introduced by Manabe–Shinagawa, we can further reduce the number of cards in certain configurations.

title: SOMA: Stack-of-Objects Manipulation using a Quadruped Robot
abstract: Executing heavy-duty physical manipulation in unpredictable environments remains a major challenge for quadrupedal robots lacking dedicated manipulators. This paper presents SOMA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for whole-body non-prehensile manipulation of multi-object stacks using a quadruped robot. Unlike traditional methods restricted to two-dimensional planar pushing, SOMA integrates explicit robot base-height control, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This capability enables the quadruped to manipulate complex payload stacks as a unified system while preventing relative sliding or tipping of upper layers. The architecture factorizes control into a high-level manipulation policy using a Simplified Structured State Space Sequence (S5) encoder to reason over long-horizon temporal history and predict bounded target tracking commands via Beta distributions, and a low-level locomotion policy that dynamically adapts leg stance configurations. In extensive simulation benchmarks, SOMA achieves a $90.3\%$ success rate for single-object reposing and up to $90.1\%$ for dynamic two-box stacks under stringent error margins ($0.05\text{ m}$ position error, $1^\circ$ orientation error). Finally, we validate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot across diverse payload masses and geometries, demonstrating active base-height adjustments to maintain traction and balance during heavy pushing tasks.

title: Sequential Learning-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network Modeling for Parameter Estimation on a Power Converter
abstract: A staged physics-informed neural network (PINN) is proposed for identifying the inductance, capacitance and parasitic resistances of a DC buck converter from time-domain data. Gradients are released in the order of L to C to rL to rC, a sequence derived from sensitivity analysis. The five-stage schedule recovers L and C to within 5% and the series ESR to 10%, while a three-stage variant attains the same accuracy 11% faster. An 84 factorial sweep confirms that the trained PINN remains accurate for simultaneous 8% perturbations of all four components, achieving a waveform RMSE of 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms-an order-of-magnitude better than a simultaneous-training baseline.

title: Confidence Based Sequential Drift Detection Under Resource Constraints
abstract: Concept Drift Detectors are the methods that are used to identify the patterns and behaviors of data that changes over time. These methods are tested separately on different datasets, which makes it difficult to compare which detector is suitable for particular situation. This paper presents the comparison of seven concept-drift detectors: ADWIN, DDM, EDDM, KSWIN, Page-Hinkley, Naive-T and a new lightweight detector called SeqConf. These seven detectors were tested on 120 simulated data streams. This experiment used two basic problems, three types of drift and twenty different random seeds for each case. Here we already know the drift points, the performance of each detector could be measured accurately. All detector used the same fixed online classifier, so that their detection performance, false alarms and computational requirements could be compared under the same conditions. SeqConf combines confidence-based monitoring, it does not require labels after deployment and uses constant memory. It uses persistence rule to reduce false alarms caused by single unusual samples. The results from 840 detector run shows that it has lowest memory usage and second lowest false alarm rate with 0.30 false alarms per 9000 samples on stationary data. Its detection rate is lowest among the seven detectors, at 12.5%. This experiment also showed that confidence-based detectors such as KSWIN, Page-Hinkley and SeqConf had difficulty detecting a gradual drift in the SEA dataset. EEDM, KSWIN and the Naïve-T baseline, produced alarms very frequently. The paper provides the complete experimental results and figures so that experiments can be repeated and verified.

title: Menuju Sistem AI yang Dapat Dijelaskan (XAI) untuk Pengalaman Pengguna yang Lebih Baik: Studi tentang Interaksi Multimodal pada Perangkat Cerdas untuk Pembelajaran Reflektif
abstract: Sistem Kecerdasan Buatan (AI) semakin terintegrasi dalam kehidupan sehari-hari melalui perangkat cerdas, namun kurangnya transparansi dan kemampuan menjelaskan (explainability) sering menjadi hambatan dalam membangun kepercayaan dan pengalaman pengguna yang bermakna. Penelitian ini mengkaji peran Explainable AI (XAI) dalam meningkatkan pengalaman pengguna melalui interaksi multimodal pada perangkat cerdas, dengan fokus pada bagaimana mekanisme penjelasan dapat mendukung pembelajaran reflektif. Melalui tinjauan literatur sistematis terhadap perkembangan terkini dalam XAI, interaksi multimodal, dan desain antarmuka, penelitian ini mengidentifikasi bahwa efektivitas XAI sangat bergantung pada bagaimana penjelasan disampaikan dan dikontekstualisasikan dalam pengalaman pengguna. Temuan menunjukkan bahwa pendekatan multimodal menggabungkan penjelasan visual, tekstual, dan auditori meningkatkan pemahaman pengguna hingga 40% dibandingkan penjelasan unimodal, sementara penjelasan adaptif yang disesuaikan dengan tingkat keahlian pengguna meningkatkan kepercayaan dan kepuasan secara signifikan. Interaksi multimodal pada perangkat cerdas memungkinkan pengguna untuk mengeksplorasi dan memahami keputusan AI melalui berbagai saluran sensorik, mendorong pembelajaran reflektif dimana pengguna tidak hanya menerima output AI tetapi juga merefleksikan proses penalaran di baliknya. Tantangan yang masih ada mencakup trade-off antara transparansi dan kejelasan, beban kognitif dari penjelasan yang berlebihan, serta kebutuhan untuk menyeimbangkan akurasi dan interpretabilitas dalam model AI. Penelitian ini menyimpulkan bahwa XAI multimodal yang dirancang dengan mempertimbangkan kebutuhan pengguna dan konteks penggunaan dapat menjadi jembatan antara kompleksitas teknis AI dan pengalaman pengguna yang intuitif dan memberdayakan, membuka jalan menuju AI yang lebih transparan, tepercaya, dan kolaboratif.

title: Pemodelan Klasifikasi Tingkat Kerusakan Peralatan Penunjang Akademik Berbasis Natural Language Processing dan Naïve Bayes
abstract: Pengelolaan laporan kerusakan peralatan akademik menghadapi permasalahan karena informasi kerusakan umumnya disampaikan dalam bentuk teks tidak terstruktur dengan variasi deskripsi yang berbeda. Kondisi tersebut menyulitkan proses identifikasi tingkat kerusakan secara konsisten dan dapat memperlambat penanganan aset. Penelitian ini bertujuan menerapkan Natural Language Processing untuk mengolah deskripsi laporan kerusakan dan menggunakan algoritma Naïve Bayes untuk mengklasifikasikan tingkat kerusakan peralatan. Data penelitian diperoleh dari laporan kerusakan pada Unit Penunjang Akademik Perawatan dan Perbaikan Politeknik Negeri Sriwijaya periode 2021–2026. Sebanyak 4.147 data laporan dikumpulkan dan melalui tahap data preparation diperoleh 2.374 data yang digunakan dalam proses klasifikasi. Pengolahan teks dilakukan melalui case folding, tokenizing, filtering, dan stemming, kemudian data direpresentasikan menggunakan pembobotan Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). Karena distribusi kelas tidak seimbang, Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) diterapkan pada data training sebelum proses klasifikasi menggunakan Naïve Bayes. Evaluasi terhadap 475 data testing menghasilkan akurasi sebesar 86,53%. Hasil tersebut menunjukkan bahwa kombinasi text preprocessing, TF-IDF, SMOTE, dan Naïve Bayes dapat diterapkan untuk mengklasifikasikan tingkat kerusakan peralatan berdasarkan teks laporan kerusakan.

Penelitian ini bertujuan menerapkan Natural Language Processing untuk mengolah deskripsi laporan kerusakan dan menggunakan algoritma Naïve Bayes untuk mengklasifikasikan tingkat kerusakan peralatan. Data penelitian diperoleh dari laporan kerusakan pada Unit Penunjang Akademik Perawatan dan Perbaikan Politeknik Negeri Sriwijaya periode 2021–2026. Sebanyak 4.147 data laporan dikumpulkan dan melalui tahap data preparation diperoleh 2.374 data yang digunakan dalam proses klasifikasi. Pengolahan teks dilakukan melalui case folding, tokenizing, filtering, dan stemming, kemudian data direpresentasikan menggunakan pembobotan Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). Karena distribusi kelas tidak seimbang, Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) diterapkan pada data training sebelum proses klasifikasi menggunakan Naïve Bayes. Evaluasi terhadap 475 data testing menghasilkan akurasi sebesar 86,53%. Hasil tersebut menunjukkan bahwa kombinasi text preprocessing, TF-IDF, SMOTE, dan Naïve Bayes dapat diterapkan untuk mengklasifikasikan tingkat kerusakan peralatan berdasarkan teks laporan kerusakan.

title: NetArray, a New Seismic Array Methodology with Example Implementation for Earthquake Early Warning
abstract: ABSTRACT Accurate seismic source location remains challenging when earthquakes occur outside or near the edges of seismic networks. Standard network methods require favorable azimuthal coverage and suffer from severe distance–depth trade-offs, whereas conventional array approaches assume planar wavefronts and are restricted to distant sources. Here, we introduce NetArray, a methodology that unifies network and array approaches within a single framework. Based on a planar–radial decomposition of interstation delays, NetArray relaxes the plane-wave assumption to explicitly account for wavefront curvature. This yields a semianalytical, velocity-model-independent cost function that jointly constrains back azimuth, epicentral distance, and horizontal slowness. After the slowness vector and epicentral distance are resolved, a velocity model is used to constrain source depth, avoiding the distance–depth trade-off inherent to network methods. Synthetic tests demonstrate that NetArray notably improves back-azimuth accuracy relative to standard array methods at distances up to several times the array aperture while providing reliable estimates of epicentral distance and depth. Compared with conventional network approaches, NetArray yields more stable solutions for out-of-network sources and provides explicit minimum and maximum distance bounds for uncertainty estimation. Application to a virtual array in the Mendocino Triple Junction region highlights NetArray’s potential for earthquake early warning systems: using a limited number of stations, the method successfully mitigates the offshore distance overestimation inherited in network approaches. These results demonstrate that NetArray provides a robust, unified framework for real-time and offline seismic source location.

title: Türkçede edebî parmak izleri: Dğal dil işleme ve makine öğrenmesi kullanarak kitap türü bulma ve yazar eşleştirme
abstract: Edebi içerik temelli yazar eşleştirme, tür sınıflandırması ve öneri sistemleri doğal dil işlemede giderek daha fazla önem kazanmaktadır. Bu çalışma, kitap metinlerini vektör uzayında temsil ederek hem sınıflandırma hem de içerik tabanlı öneri yapabilen bir sistem sunmaktadır. Türkçe romanlardan oluşan kapsamlı bir veri kümesi derlenmiş, ön işlemden geçirilmiş ve Doc2Vec algoritması kullanılarak yüksek boyutlu vektörlere dönüştürülmüştür. Genellenebilirliği sağlamak amacıyla, her bir yazarın test kümesinde yer almasını garanti eden özel bir eğitim/test bölme stratejisi uygulanmıştır. Elde edilen belge vektörleri, Doğrusal Destek Vektör Makinesi Sınıflandırıcısı, Lojistik Regresyon, Rastgele Orman, Gauss Naive Bayes ve En Yakın Komşular gibi sınıflandırıcılarla yazar ve tür tespitinde kullanılmıştır. Deneysel sonuçlar, ilk iki yöntemin hem tür hem de yazar tahmininde diğer üç yönteme göre daha yüksek performans gösterdiğini ortaya koymuştur. Bu çalışma ayrıca, geleneksel kosinüs benzerliğinin ötesine geçen özgün bir sınıflandırma yaklaşımı önermektedir. Geliştirilen yöntem, okuyucunun daha önce beğendiği eserlerle benzer anlatım tarzına sahip kitapları önererek daha az bilinen yazarların görünürlüğünün artırılmasına katkı sağlamaktadır. Araştırma, belge gömme tabanlı yöntemlerin dijital beşerî bilimler ve öneri sistemlerinde etkili bir biçimde uygulanabileceğini göstermektedir.

title: Logical CCZ state cultivation
abstract: Logical CCZ states enable Toffoli gates, a central building block of fault-tolerant quantum arithmetic. We introduce an end-to-end protocol for direct CCZ-state preparation on bivariate tricycle and bicycle (BT/BB) codes. Our factory combines the cup-product CCZ gates native to BT codes with two novel ingredients, both enabled by engineering the logical coupling between BT and BB codes through projection-preserving lifts. Index-2 lifted BB ancillas enable selective $Z$-basis initialization, allowing the native cup-product gates to directly prepare two disjoint logical CCZ states. The prepared CCZ states are faithfully transferred to index-3 lifted BB memories with high code distance. We use decoder-based postselection to obtain high-fidelity output states with low overhead. We perform exact simulations of our factory under a circuit-level noise model motivated by neutral-atom hardware, obtaining joint infidelities of $1.84\times10^{-5}$ at $21.94\%$ acceptance and $4.10\times10^{-7}$ at $8.89\%$ acceptance for single-qubit, CZ, and CCZ error rates of $0.01\%$, $0.1\%$, and $0.5\%$, respectively. At the output-infidelity target of our smallest factory, its estimated spacetime cost per CCZ state is lower than that of $T$-state cultivation followed by CCZ conversion, providing an efficient route to logical CCZ states for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
abstract: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.

title: SWE-Nexus: Automated Composition of Software Engineering Tasks from Test Execution
abstract: Historical code changes provide convenient task boundaries, but do not identify which production functions selected tests exercise or support composing validated behaviors beyond a single change. We present SWE-Nexus, a fully automated pipeline that constructs repository-level implementation tasks from test execution. Four construction agents select tests, adapt tracing and evaluation protocols to each repository, and generate behavioral specifications. For each selected test file, tracing records an observed execution footprint of production function bodies. A scope is retained only if all expected scoring points pass in the original repository and masking the traced bodies causes at least one failure or error. Compatible scopes are composed deterministically, with shared functions counted once and every constituent test file revalidated under the complete combined mask. The benchmark contains 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages, including 116 atomic and 484 composite tasks. We evaluate 12 models under three agent scaffolds. The best configuration resolves 37.8% of tasks in one attempt, and scope-weighted scoring measures partial recovery. SWE-Nexus enables task construction from validated behavior beyond individual historical changes.

title: LiFi: LiDAR Generation from Multi-View Images via Geometric and Semantic Collaborative Guidance
abstract: Generating LiDAR point clouds from multi-view camera images is a valuable task with applications in controllable data synthesis, cross-modal simulation and various perception tasks. However, most existing methods are not specifically designed for this task, and the quality of their generated LiDAR remains limited. Moreover, these methods typically focus only on semantic cues in images or generate LiDAR from a monocular camera image. In this work, we introduce LiFi (LiDAR From images), a dedicated framework for generating visually and geometrically aligned LiDAR scenes from multi-view camera images. LiFi guides the latent diffusion process through two complementary branches: geometry and semantics. The geometry branch constructs scene features from images through a reverse sampling algorithm and an uncertainty-aware geometric encoder combined with DepthAnything3, whereas the semantic branch provides high-level semantic representations via a cross-view interaction module. We further introduce a dual-branch balanced classifier-free guidance (CFG) strategy, which enhances the model's conditional generation capability while preserving the independent learning and collaborative controllability of the two branches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiFi outperforms state-of-the-art methods in generating high-fidelity LiDAR scenes. The code will be publicly available at: https://github.com/szzhou88/LiFi.

title: LED-BENCH: A Benchmark for Large-format Engineering Drawing Understanding
abstract: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. Extensive evaluation of 11 representative multimodal large language models, including 8 proprietary models and 3 open-source models, reveals substantial remaining difficulty: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves 52.65% average accuracy, performance varies across engineering domains, and all evaluated models perform worse on questions requiring broader evidence integration. These results highlight fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings as persistent challenges for current multimodal models.

title: Speaking Longer Than Learned: Training-Free Long-Form Generation for Full-Stream Text-to-Speech
abstract: Recent full-stream text-to-speech (TTS) models enable low-latency personalized synthesis as input text arrives. However, sustaining generation beyond the lengths seen during training without additional training remains largely unexplored. We systematically analyze VoXtream2, which extends generation by periodically discarding past context while retaining the acoustic prompt. We find that this strategy does not prevent degradation: pronunciation accuracy deteriorates near the end of the training range due to the range of positions in which the model operates rather than the loss of past context, while speaker similarity gradually declines throughout generation. Based on these findings, we propose two training-free modifications that reduce the attention window and strengthen attention to the acoustic prompt. Experiments show that these modifications preserve pronunciation accuracy and speaker similarity throughout long-form generation while retaining the naturalness of the original model. Ablations further show complementary effects of the two modifications.

title: Analisis Sentimen Ulasan Pengguna Aplikasi Layanan Kesehatan Digital Di Indonesia Menggunakan BERT Dan Support Vector Machine
abstract: The development of digital health services in Indonesia has generated numerous user reviews that can be analyzed to identify user perceptions of service quality. This study aims to analyze the sentiment of user reviews of digital health service applications and compare the performance of BERT and Support Vector Machine (SVM). The dataset consisted of 13,456 reviews from Halodoc, Alodokter, and KlikDokter collected from 2022 to 2024. The research stages included data collection, preprocessing, sentiment labeling, classification, and model evaluation. IndoBERT was implemented through fine-tuning, while SVM used TF-IDF features with Grid Search optimization. The results showed that IndoBERT achieved an accuracy of 93.52% and a macro F1-score of 92.23%, while SVM achieved an accuracy of 87.14% and a macro F1-score of 84.71%. These results indicate that IndoBERT outperformed SVM in classifying sentiment in digital health service application reviews.

title: λBLL∞: Beyond polynomial time in presence of randomized computation
abstract: In this thesis we introduce the λBLL∞ calculus, a purely functional graded calculus designed for the formal analysis of mixed complexity probabilistic computation. Building upon the foundations of Bounded Linear Logic (BLL), we propose two significant extensions: the removal of stateful effects in favour of a pure functional semantics, and the expansion of the resource-accounting algebra to include exponential grades and a symbolic infinite limit. We provide a complete formal characterization of the system, including a small step operational semantics based on a sub-stochastic monad to correctly capture both probabilistic branching and potential divergence. We establish the internal consistency of λBLL∞ through exhaustive proofs of substitution and subject reduction. Furthermore, we present a soundness theorem demonstrating that the grades assigned by the type system serves as a sound complexity certificate for membership in PTIME and EXPTIME fragments. Finally, we develop a simplified logical metric based on statistical distance and apply it to cryptographic case studies. We demonstrate that λBLL∞ can formally characterize the “Security Gap” of a protocol, proving that the resource grade of an observer context serves as the definitive boundary for computational indistinguishability.

title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) Innovations for Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Social Well-Being in Nigeria
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a strong tool for tackling worldwide issues, including the United Nations SDGs. This paper investigates how AI innovations can be used to further the SDGs and improve societal welfare in Nigeria. Primary data gathered through questionnaires, surveys, and discussions with stakeholders from government bodies, private enterprises, and schools were used. The study focuses on three SDG targets: reducing poverty, delivering quality education, and ensuring affordable healthcare. Using chi-square analysis, the research found a notable positive link between AI tools and higher earnings in cities, but no meaningful effect in rural zones. It also observed improved educational access in both urban and remote locations. Moreover, AI-driven mobile health apps significantly boosted healthcare access in cities, though not in rural areas. While these results offer a guide for using AI to promote fairness and economic progress in Nigeria, the paper also looks at obstacles such as poor infrastructure, lack of skills, and ethical issues. It recommends that the Nigerian government extend electricity and internet connections to underserved regions, offer subsidies for AI tools, provide digital training, and foster public-private partnerships to roll out AI solutions in education, health, and poverty reduction.

title: Decisions and Feedback Across the Lifecycle of Hardware-Efficient Language Model Systems
abstract: Hardware-efficient Transformer-based language-model systems make consequential choices across development/adaptation, deployment preparation, and runtime/serving, yet mechanism-centric organization can obscure their dependencies. This critical survey uses two-stage Scopus retrieval, structured screening, detailed assessment of eligible cross-lifecycle evidence, and targeted contextual enrichment. Its decision-centric framework organizes Evidence → Decision → Action relations through lifecycle locus, evidence, action, hardware role, timescale, forward coupling, and feedback. The reconciled evidence shows upstream-to-runtime coupling through prepared choice spaces, conditional capabilities, and profile/information interfaces, which may overlap. Feedback is distinguished as search/configuration feedback (FB-S), runtime-local feedback (FB-R), operational evidence reused upstream (FB-O), and strict lifecycle closure (FB-C). Industrial RAG verifies FB-O through operational records reused in upstream parameter-efficient adaptation; the inspected evidence does not establish subsequent deployment of the revised artifact with an observed operational consequence. No source in the reconciled corpus was confirmed as strict FB-C. Distinguishing hardware-evidence origin (H_SPEC, H_PROFILE, H_LIVE) from functional role (H0–H4), the seven-dimensional taxonomy supports structural comparison and a corpus-bounded agenda addressing upstream evidence reuse, operationally validated closure, hardware evidence crossing upstream, and cross-timescale escalation. It does not imply mechanism rankings or field-wide prevalence.

title: Study 6: Mechanism and a remedy for converging change requests (registered during data generation)
abstract: This is the analysis plan for Study 6, a follow-up to a preregistered study of how requests change the diversity of large language model answers (https://osf.io/wzcgq). Study 6 asks two questions. First, do answers to a request for "something from a different group" follow the model's context-free preferences, once the current group is removed? Second, does linking the change to a detail of the conversation keep answers diverse across conversations? The plan was fixed before any Study 6 data existed. It is registered while data generation is under way and before any Study 6 analysis has been run.

title: MSP: Modality Self-Play for Training Multimodal LLMs Without Paired Cross-Modal Data
abstract: Large multimodal models have achieved remarkable progress by scaling model capacity and training on massive paired multimodal data. However, this paradigm introduces a fundamental bottleneck: aligned multimodal datasets are expensive to curate, difficult to scale across diverse modality combinations, and increasingly constrain further progress. We introduce Modality Self-Play (MSP), a training framework for multimodal foundation models based on proxy-mediated modality composition. Instead of relying on paired cross-modal data, MSP uses anchor-supporting proxy textual descriptions of unseen modalities as semantic bridges during training. Given an observed modality (e.g., image or audio), the model generates proxy descriptions for complementary unseen modalities, which are then encoded and aligned with the observed modality through learned bridges, enabling cross-modal interaction without real paired non-text supervision. Our central hypothesis is that proxy text, combined with contrastively trained pretrained encoders, provides sufficient semantic structure for multimodal composition to emerge. We show that MSP enables zero-shot modality composition: models trained only with a real anchor modality and accompanying proxy descriptions can integrate and reason over multiple modalities at inference time despite never observing real paired non-text data during training. Empirically, MSP achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on multiple multimodal benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate that learned bridges improve alignment, while anchor-supporting proxy descriptions enable effective cross-modal composition. MSP removes the need for real paired non-text (e.g., audio-vision) supervision, while continuing to rely on modality-text pairs, pretrained contrastive encoders, and modality-distribution bridge calibration.

title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.

title: Weighted Adjoint Matching: Finetuning Flow Matching Models with Time-Dependent Control Cost
abstract: We introduce Weighted Adjoint Matching, a method to finetune a pretrained diffusion or flow matching model given a differentiable reward. We derive it from Adjoint Matching, which reformulates finetuning as a stochastic optimal control problem with a quadratic control cost. Building on the observation that these models generate coarse features before fine details, we place a time-dependent weight on the control cost. A high cost early in the generative process preserves balance and diversity in the coarse features, which carry most of the semantics, while a low cost at the end lets the model increase the reward by refining details. We prove that our method is equivalent to maximizing the reward under time-varying Kullback--Leibler regularization on the generative paths. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and on MNIST show a better tradeoff between reward and mode balance than Adjoint Matching.

title: Adaptive and Proximal Federated Optimization for Transferable Network Intrusion Detection
abstract: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) based on deep learning often fail to detect attack classes that are absent from training data, limiting their robustness against zero-day threats. This property called transferability across attack classes, remains underexplored especially in federated learning (FL) settings where data heterogeneity and client drift pose additional challenges. Prior work (TabFIDS) showed that FedAvg combined with bootstrapping and temporal averaging improves transferability for cross-device NIDS. In this paper, we explore whether other federated optimizers can do better. We compare two optimizers inspired by FedAdam and FedProx against the FedAvg baseline on the CIC-IDS 2017 dataset using an 11-client federated setup, sweep 10 hyperparameter configurations, and contrast two data-balancing strategies: bootstrapping and SMOTE. Using the count of client pairs whose transferred-model accuracy exceeds 70% as our primary metric (following TabFIDS), the proximal optimizer with a strong regularization term yields 48 transferable pairs versus 42 for FedAvg, while the adaptive optimizer with an aggressive server learning rate yields 46 pairs. SMOTE improves per-pair accuracy over bootstrapping but reduces breadth, revealing a depth-vs-breadth trade-off: high accuracy on a few client pairs versus moderate accuracy across most. These results indicate that the choice of federated optimizer, the rule by which client updates are regularized and aggregated into the global model, is very important for federated NIDS.

title: FPV-CRASH: A Dataset for Offline Crash Moment Localization in Drone First-Person-View Videos
abstract: Crash Moment Localization aims to localize the major physical impact that interrupts controlled flight in an onboard first-person-view (FPV) video recorded by a drone, thereby providing a temporal reference for retrospective crash analysis in aerial robotics. However, existing crash-video datasets predominantly target surveillance or dash-camera footage, and their annotation schemes and task formulations are not designed for temporal localization of the major physical impact in UAV onboard FPV videos. To address this gap, we present FPV-CRASH, a dataset and fixed-protocol reference evaluation for offline Crash Moment Localization in drone FPV videos. FPV-CRASH contains 1,052 drone FPV clips (526 Crash and 526 Normal); each Crash clip has a single-frame reference annotation for the Crash Moment, and every clip is paired with four English captions automatically generated from sampled frames and the known Crash/Normal label. Normal clips carry no timestamp target and provide training-time background supervision. The captions support an auxiliary Text-to-Video Retrieval task, whereas localization inference remains video-only. We further provide a heatmap-based reference model that estimates a continuous Crash Moment timestamp from sparsely sampled frames. Under the fixed, non-source-disjoint clip-level protocol, the reference model reduces MAE from 1.12 s for the strongest fixed timing-prior baseline to 0.56 s (a 50% relative reduction) and achieves a median absolute error (MedAE) of 0.33 s; the fraction of clips localized within 0.5 s rises from 37.14% to 65.71%. The release includes annotations, available source video identifiers and URLs, clipping metadata, fixed split lists, and preprocessing code so that the reportable portion can be reconstructed without redistributing source footage. At submission time, all source-compilation URLs remained accessible.
