title: Deep-Learning-Based Assessment of Breast Arterial Calcification on Mammography: Technical Validation, Cardiovascular Prognostic Value, and Clinical Translation—A Narrative Review
abstract: Breast arterial calcification (BAC) is a manifestation of medial arterial calcification frequently detected incidentally on screening mammography. Increasing evidence suggests that BAC may also serve as a marker of cardiovascular risk. This narrative review critically synthesizes the evidence on artificial intelligence (AI)-based detection, segmentation, and quantification of BAC. It also evaluates the cardiovascular prognostic significance of automatically quantified BAC and examines the requirements for clinical translation. A targeted literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted for English-language publications available from database inception through 3 September 2026, with additional studies identified from reference lists. Deep-learning approaches included convolutional neural networks, U-Net-derived segmentation architectures, transfer-learning models, and semi-supervised methods. Reported technical performance varied according to task and validation strategy. Representative segmentation models achieved Dice/F1 scores ranging from 0.666 to 0.756 and Jaccard indices from 0.581 to 0.614. Case-level BAC detection achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of up to 0.95–0.96 in selected test cohorts. However, external validation, learning-curve reporting, multivendor evaluation, and robustness assessment remained inconsistent. Prognostic studies demonstrated graded associations between automated BAC burden and cardiovascular outcomes. In a cohort of 21,514 women without known cardiovascular disease, age-adjusted BAC burden was associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) among women classified as low risk, with adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) of 1.66 and 2.31 for BAC below and above the age-specific median, respectively. In 123,762 women from two healthcare systems, MACE risk increased progressively with BAC burden after adjustment using the Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs (PREVENT) equations, reaching approximately 2.8- to 3.3-fold higher risk with severe BAC. Nevertheless, incremental predictive improvement may be small—in one study, the addition of BAC changed the 5-year AUC from 0.645 to 0.646. Overall, available evidence supports the feasibility of scalable AI-based BAC assessment and demonstrates consistent associations between AI-quantified BAC and cardiovascular outcomes. However, technical performance and independent prognostic associations alone do not establish clinical utility. Standardized BAC definitions, genuinely independent external validation, and prospective implementation studies are required before BAC-guided cardiovascular management can be recommended.

title: Sprachmodelle im Wandel : Wie viel KI passt heutzutage unter den Schreibtisch? Was Sprachmodelle leisten - und was ihr lokaler Betrieb braucht
abstract: Leistungsfähige Sprachmodelle lassen sich zunehmend auch auf lokalen, selbst betriebenen Systemen ausführen. Der Vortrag beleuchtet ausgewählte Entwicklungsschritte von frühen statistischen Sprachmodellen über neuronale Netze und Transformer bis zum heutigen Stand. Im Mittelpunkt stehen unter anderem Fortschritte in Bezug auf Architektur und Training, welche die Fähigkeiten der Modelle erweitert haben. Zudem wird aufgezeigt, wie der Zugang zu Modellgewichten, geeignete Software und speichersparende Verfahren zunehmend den lokalen Betrieb von Sprachmodellen ermöglicht haben. Ergänzend werden die aktuellen Möglichkeiten und Grenzen der Nutzung von lokalen Sprachmodellen knapp dargestellt.

title: matrans: an R package for parameter-transfer learning of multi-source cancer prognosis data
abstract: The rapid growth of multi-source molecular profiling data has created new opportunities for integrative cancer prognosis modeling. However, heterogeneity across datasets often limits model generalizability. Transfer learning provides a powerful strategy to leverage auxiliary information from related source domains. Parameter-transfer learning based on frequentist model averaging is a leading-edge approach that has been widely used in practice. Nevertheless, the lack of accessible and user-friendly software has limited its broader adoption. We introduce matrans , an R package that implements a parameter-transfer learning framework based on frequentist model averaging within a semiparametric setting. The proposed procedure circumvents a separate source-selection step by adaptively weighting the target and source estimators according to their predictive performance on the target data. Furthermore, the source models can be fitted locally, and the transfer process requires only source-level parameter estimates rather than the centralized pooling of individual-level source data. Simulation studies and a real-world multi-source cancer prognosis case study demonstrate that matrans achieves robust estimation accuracy, improved predictive performance, and high computational efficiency. The package is freely available at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=matrans . matrans offers a convenient and efficient tool for parameter-transfer learning from multi-source cancer prognosis datasets, bridging the gap between methodological advances and practical biomedical applications.

title: Federated multimodal home school collaborative dance intervention for inclusive preschool education with privacy preserving and explainable AI framework
abstract: Inclusive preschool dance intervention is a high-impact yet methodologically difficult educational scenario. Effective intervention requires precise movement analysis, longitudinal home–school collaboration, and communication outputs that teachers and caregivers can directly act on. At the same time, child data governance imposes strict constraints on centralizing raw videos, behavior logs, and family reports. Existing systems typically optimize only one axis, such as model accuracy or platform usability, but do not provide a unified technical and evaluation framework that addresses educational efficacy, privacy, fairness, and interpretability together. This paper develops a federated multimodal framework for inclusive preschool dance education, with explicit links between model design and educational decision requirements. The method combines pose-sequence encoding, teacher-record embedding, parent-text representation, and interaction-log modeling under incomplete-modality conditions. Reliability-aware fusion is coupled with fairness regularization and differential-privacy training. A constrained recommendation module translates model outputs into role-specific guidance for teachers and caregivers while preserving evidence traceability. To evaluate this system under realistic intervention conditions, we define a 16-week three-arm cluster-randomized protocol and an eight-experiment matrix covering intervention effect, retention, mediation, fairness, ablation, robustness, privacy–utility trade-off, and cross-school transfer. The complete system was implemented and evaluated under the study protocol described in Sect. 4 . All numerical values in Tables 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 and 10 ; Figs. 5 , 6 , 7 and 8 are retained from the completed study and model experiments; no values were simulated or generated during this revision. The empirical results show the largest motor-skill and social-inclusion gains for HomeSchool-AI, while the ablation, robustness, privacy–utility, and cross-school analyses provide complementary evidence for the proposed framework.

title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition
abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.

title: A Strong Harness Narrows the Model Gap: A Comparative Evaluation for Legislative Document-to-XML Conversion
abstract: Legal-content reproduction requires matching the source exactly in section hierarchy, verbatim text, citations, and amendment spans; a dropped citation or mislabeled amendment carries into the products lawyers rely on. We report an industrial pipeline converting U.S. state legislation into strict, schema-constrained XML, and hypothesize that its accuracy comes from harness engineering, the deterministic tooling built around a model, more than the model itself. Our controlled ablation crosses three harnesses (zero-shot, a single tool-using agent, and a decomposed multi-agent pipeline) with three Claude models on 153 gold bills from two jurisdictions. The harness narrows the model gap: the weakest model in the full pipeline beats the strongest model alone (0.948 versus 0.806, paired bootstrap p less than 0.001). Because the two agentic harnesses share identical tools, their gap comes from orchestration: decomposition plus the persisted state and per-agent context it brings. Across four scored dimensions, the model spread at zero-shot (0.68 to 0.81) narrows to 0.95 at the full pipeline; the residual sits almost entirely in citation normalization, where the canonical identifier is retrieved from an external authority rather than generated from the weights, so a deterministic lookup tool supplies the exactness that a larger model does not.

title: LabCompiler: A Framework for Verifiable Human-Machine Laboratory Execution from Imperfect Protocols
abstract: Closing the loop of AI-driven science requires reliably translating natural-language protocols into executable laboratory workflows despite protocol defects and heterogeneous hardware. Existing approaches often couple scientific interpretation with device-specific code generation, making errors difficult to localize and limiting reuse across laboratory platforms. We introduce LabCompiler, a robust protocol-to-execution framework that transforms imperfect natural-language protocols into verifiable human-machine workflows. Its protocol firewall diagnoses and repairs defects before compilation while preserving unaffected content, guided by troubleshooting knowledge accumulated through perturbation-guided self-evolution. A two-level, device-agnostic graph representation separates experimental semantics from hardware-specific implementation and supports capability-based device assignment with coordinated human execution. We further introduce a protocol recovery benchmark covering four controlled perturbation types and naturally occurring errors collected from protocols written by iGEM participants. Experiments show that LabCompiler outperforms frontier LLMs in protocol error correction while enabling coordinated human-machine execution across heterogeneous, partially automated laboratory settings.

title: Can We Believe AI Peer Review?
abstract: As large language models become widely used in scientific review and manuscript revision, AI scores are increasingly serving as feedback for assessing paper quality and guiding edits. Yet whether a single AI score reliably reflects the reviewer's judgment, and whether revision gains based on that score are endorsed by other reviewers, remain understudied. Using 200 papers from ICLR 2025 and 2026 and approximately 14,000 AI reviews, we study score reliability, score-distribution estimation, and cross-model agreement on revision gains. Repeated reviews fluctuate even under identical conditions. Finer-grained scoring protocols reduce score variance but also systematically shift mean scores, while the gains assigned to manuscript revisions depend strongly on the reviewer.

title: ELASTIC Newsletter #5: Into the Final Stretch
abstract: The fifth issue of the ELASTIC project newsletter marks the project's final stretch towards its conclusion in February 2027, as the consortium moves from mid-term results to system-level integration and validation. This issue covers ELASTIC's participation at EuCNC & 6G Summit 2026 in Málaga (Booth 76), where both demonstrators were shown live, and the technical plenary in Belgrade. It presents the project's integration focus: secure WebAssembly orchestration with Propeller, remote attestation and confidential workload migration, eBPF-based security, federated learning and AI-powered intrusion detection. Further highlights include a general-audience article on the project, the component booklet now on Zenodo, ELASTIC's co-organisation of the WACE 2026 workshop at ACM Middleware (Tarragona, 14–18 December 2026), the recording and slides of the joint ELASTIC & 6G-PATH webinar, collaborations with SAFE-6G and 6G-PATH, and recent scientific publications at KDD 2026 (Lasso) and ARES 2026 (WasmStone).

title: AI-Mediated Personal Infrastructure: From AI-Built Apps to AI-Coordinated Personal Systems
abstract: The future personal computing environment may take the form of an AI coordination layer over existing software rather than another comprehensive application. This note proposes AI-Mediated Personal Infrastructure (AMPI): a design framework that retains tools' specialized capabilities and coordinates them around a person's goals through semantic interpretation, tool invocation, persistent state, and verifiable execution. AI helps decide what information means and which system should perform a task. Conventional programs retain responsibility for bounded access, durable records, permissions, execution checks, and recovery. AcademicWorkspace, the author's privately operated academic workflow environment, grounds the framework in a concrete practice. A sanitized historical archiving episode illustrates how source identity, user decisions, and generated interpretations remain distinct. AMPI includes direct interfaces, command-line tools, and optional GUI agents; it requires no particular operating system, model, or new interface. Its contribution is an explicit synthesis of design commitments and an implementation-informed account, building on substantial prior work. The single-person case establishes neither general effectiveness nor historical priority. Concept note / position statement; not peer reviewed. Sole author: Omica Chow. AI assistance for research support, code inspection, organization, writing, translation and production is disclosed in the manuscript; AI is not an author. This record archives the unchanged AMPI v0.1 release files first made public on GitHub on 14 October 2026. GitHub Release: AMPI v0.1. Original materials: CC BY 4.0.

title: Cross-Comparison of Ground Observations, CAMS Estimates, and Linke-Model Irradiance for Photovoltaic System Design in Sahelian Niger
abstract: Reliable solar-resource inputs are essential for photovoltaic (PV) and hybrid-system design, but temporal matching and measurement traceability require scrutiny where reference records are scarce. This study compares SM206-SOLAR ground observations, Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) Radiation Service v4.6 estimates and Linke-model irradiance for Dosso, Niger, in May and August 2021. The CAMS v4.6 dataset documents the coordinates, altitude, UTC intervals and irradiation units. Ground records at nominal local observation times were paired with centered 30-minute CAMS means constructed from adjacent 15-minute intervals. Requiring both intervals to have Reliability = 1 retained 339 and 320 pairs, respectively, distributed over 31 dates in each month. Statistics were calculated across daily means formed from identical retained times in the two series. Mean ground and CAMS irradiances were 881.31 and 627.71 W m -2 in May, and 696.29 and 530.66 W m -2 in August. Ground-minus-CAMS mean differences were +253.59 W m -2 (+40.40%) and +165.64 W m -2 (+31.21%); root-mean-square differences were 268.28 and 190.73 W m -2 , with correlations of 0.620 and 0.898. Sensitivity checks using preceding or following intervals, or retaining lower-reliability intervals, did not remove the positive mean differences. Six-point Linke comparisons on 1 May and 1 August gave root-mean-square differences of 347.70 and 278.76 W m -2 . The CAMS product identity and temporal aggregation are explicitly documented, but undocumented sensor calibration and orientation, instantaneous-versus-interval sampling and limited clear-sky characterization prevent ranking the sources by accuracy. The results support qualification of irradiance inputs; they do not quantify PV-yield or system-sizing errors.

title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
abstract: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

title: When Correctness Feedback Erases Evidence: Phase-Separated Completeness Auditing in Verus
abstract: Correctness feedback suppresses the very evidence that specification-completeness auditing is designed to uncover: programs that satisfy a written contract but violate intended behavior. We demonstrate this objective reversal on 12 Verus/Rust tasks across four model families under matched call budgets. Independent no-feedback discovery more than doubles certified-witness yield relative to IntentShield's corrective-feedback loop (59.0% versus 27.1%). A format-matched iterative control places the larger share of this gap in feedback content, not independent restarts. The advantage holds in every model family and survives parser repair. A separate phase-separated execution matches the aggregate yield without reusing responses; most certified witnesses also fail held-out cases. Preserving these witnesses delivers stronger specification repair: Phase-Revised contracts achieve 81.3% implementation success, versus 62.5% for IS-Revised, with Direct-Revised close behind. Both no-feedback witness sources substantially outperform weakened contracts. The effect does not reproduce in the available Dafny and Lean evaluations, establishing an empirical boundary around the studied Verus/Rust workflow. Completeness auditing and correctness repair have opposing immediate objectives. Preserve and certify the admitted failure before repairing it.

Independent no-feedback discovery more than doubles certified-witness yield relative to IntentShield's corrective-feedback loop (59.0% versus 27.1%). A format-matched iterative control places the larger share of this gap in feedback content, not independent restarts. The advantage holds in every model family and survives parser repair. A separate phase-separated execution matches the aggregate yield without reusing responses; most certified witnesses also fail held-out cases. Preserving these witnesses delivers stronger specification repair: Phase-Revised contracts achieve 81.3% implementation success, versus 62.5% for IS-Revised, with Direct-Revised close behind. Both no-feedback witness sources substantially outperform weakened contracts. The effect does not reproduce in the available Dafny and Lean evaluations, establishing an empirical boundary around the studied Verus/Rust workflow. Completeness auditing and correctness repair have opposing immediate objectives. Preserve and certify the admitted failure before repairing it.

title: Physics-Shaped, Not Physical: Auditing Physics-Guided Underwater Image Restoration
abstract: Physics-guided networks for underwater image restoration predict transmission and backscatter and invert the image-formation model, yet rarely test whether this physics does any work. We audit one representative design, PhysGuide-Net, with four controlled experiments: five-seed ablations on UIEB with zero-shot evaluation on the complete LSUI (4279 pairs) and AUIED3K (3000 pairs) sets; a data-efficiency study with a capacity-matched control that removes the formation model; and a validation of the predicted maps against measured range on Sea-thru. With all 800 training images the physics module gives no zero-shot gain (mean PSNR differences of at most 0.16 dB; all 95% intervals include zero) at 3.4x the FLOPs. With 80 images it helps more (+0.65 dB on UIEB, +1.48 dB on AUIED3K; seed-to-seed s.d. on AUIED3K from 1.3 to 0.5 dB), although not individually significant after correction, and the control does not reproduce this (0.8-1.0 dB lower). Yet the predicted transmission does not behave like a physical quantity: its correlation with range is no stronger than for the range map of a different image (pooled difference +0.02, versus -0.06 for the dark-channel prior), and a Beer-Lambert fit explains 0.4% of its variance. The effect of the module also changes sign with degradation severity between datasets. The benefit thus comes from a physics-shaped inductive bias, not from physics. We further show that single-run ablations can reverse sign and document implementation defects that invalidate loss ablations.

title: Robustness of multivariate longitudinal finite mixture models to covariance misspecification
abstract: Multivariate longitudinal finite mixture models can identify subjects following similar developmental trajectories across multiple outcomes. Their use for this purpose is increasing, yet they are often analysed using software defaults or by restricting the covariance structure to aid model convergence. This study ascertains, through simulation, the effects of within-outcome variance-covariance misspecification under data conditions typically faced in practice. The performance of multivariate group-based trajectory models, latent class growth analysis, and covariance pattern growth mixture models is compared in terms of enumeration, classification, and class recovery. We show that restricted covariances, exacerbated by low class separation, can lead to poor class enumeration. Moreover, despite correctly specifying the number of classes a priori, variations in model performance across conditions emerge. An empirical data set is used to illustrate differences between the models in terms of enumeration and class recovery.

title: FRM: Felix Runtime Module — papers and results
abstract: Papers and results for FRM, the Felix Runtime Module, a bounded recursive self-improvement runtime tested as FELIX-C3 against a published Level-4 definition, together with a companion preregistered study of transfer to real bugs from QuixBugs and HumanEvalFix, and an earlier preprint on the FELIX v4 self-evolving organism. Each release of this record archives the GitHub repository recurse-root/FRMDevelopment. To cite a paper, use that paper's own DOI, listed in the repository README.

title: EVALUATION OF THE INFLUENCE OF METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION ON PROCUREMENT EFFICIENCY AND PERFORMANCE OF SOLAR ENERGY PROJECTS IN NIGERIA
abstract: Nigeria, endowed with abundant solar radiation averaging 5.54 kWh/m²/day, faces a paradoxical energy crisis characterized by persistent grid unreliability and limited electricity access affecting approximately 90 million citizens. While solar photovoltaic (PV) technology presents a viable pathway toward sustainable electrification, project success hinges critically on the quality and utilization of meteorological information throughout the procurement lifecycle. This study examines the influence of meteorological data on procurement efficiency and project performance in Nigeria's solar energy sector. Through a systematic review of recent empirical studies, techno-economic assessments, and meteorological modeling approaches, the analysis reveals that accurate weather information fundamentally shapes system design optimization, technology selection, financial modeling, and operational planning. The study identifies significant challenges including dysfunctional meteorological stations, limited ground-based radiation measurements, and insufficient integration of climate variability considerations into procurement frameworks. Drawing on evidence from PVSyst simulations, HOMER Pro analyses, and machine learning forecasting models across Nigeria's diverse climatic zones, this study demonstrates that meteorological-informed procurement can enhance performance ratios by 12–15%, reduce levelized cost of energy to competitive levels, and improve investment returns. The findings underscore the imperative for developing robust meteorological infrastructure, adopting weather-aware optimization frameworks, and integrating climate risk assessment into solar energy procurement policies to accelerate Nigeria's energy transition.

title: Mobius x finitude de simetria (conjectura)
abstract: Esta nota técnica compara, no domínio discreto de 5 bits [0, 31], duas funções de pareamento: a inversão da ordem dos bits R(x) (Modelo Möbius) e f(x) = 31 − x (Finitude de Simetria / Efeito de Dobra, equivalente a NOT(x)). O domínio é representado pela lista binária convencional de base 32 (notação NC, de 00000 a 11111, com peso posicional da direita para a esquerda) e a validação é feita pela valoração de Hamming: distância dH(x, g(x)) e peso w(x). Ambas as funções são involuções, mas apenas f produz dH = 5 (distância máxima) em 32/32 casos, o que equivale à soma constante x + f(x) = 31e à ausência de pontos fixos. A função R produz dH ∈ {0, 2, 4}, nunca 5, com 8 pontos fixos (dH = 0).

title: ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORD-BASED PREDICTIVE APPROACHES FOR HOSPITAL READMISSION: A STRUCTURED REVIEW OF SOCIOECONOMIC VARIABLES AND ALGORITHMIC EQUITY
abstract: Background: Hospital readmission rates are often used to judge the quality of care and how well healthcare systems are working. Predictive models based on electronic health records (EHRs) can help estimate which patients are at higher risk, but when they don’t properly reflect socioeconomic realities, they can unintentionally reinforce existing inequalities (Obermeyer et al., 2019). This review looks at how well these EHR-based models predict 30-day readmissions, how Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) are included, and what this means for fairness and health equity in real-world use. Methodology: A structured literature review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar. It included peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2026, focusing on model validation studies, retrospective cohort analyses, and research on bias and fairness in predictive healthcare models. Results: Synthesis reveals that incorporating unstructured and structured SDOH variables yields mixed impacts on discriminatory performance (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve changes ranging from -0.01 to +0.04), yet significantly rectifies systemic algorithmic underestimation of risk for marginalized demographics. Unadjusted models consistently show racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic bias, often because they rely on proxy variables embedded in historical healthcare data (Gianfrancesco et al., 2018). As a result, preventive transition-of-care resources can be systematically directed away from the patients who need them most (Pierson et al., 2021). Conclusion: To make predictive healthcare tools truly useful in practice, it is not enough to focus only on accuracy. They also need to account for fairness, real clinical context, and the actual consequences of their use in everyday healthcare settings (Wiens et al., 2019). Policy-level interventions must mandate standardized SDOH extraction alongside equity-focused calibration algorithms before widespread clinical deployment (Ghassemi et al., 2021).

title: แผนธรกจระบบบรหารลกคาสมพนธสำหรบตจำหนายสนคาอตโนมตดวยเทคโนโลยจดจำใบหนา
authors: จุลเพชร บุญจันทร์
abstract: อุตสาหกรรมค้าปลีกไร้พนักงานของประเทศไทยกำลังเติบโตอย่างต่อเนื่องจากแนวโน้มของผู้บริโภคที่อยู่ในสังคมเมืองต้องการความสะดวกสบายและการชำระค่าสินค้าแบบไร้เงินสด ที่ทำให้ลูกค้าหันมาซื้อสินค้าผ่านตู้จำหน่ายสินค้าอัตโนมัติ (Vending machine) มากขึ้น ตลาดนี้มีมูลค่ากว่า 11.2 พันล้านบาท และมีแนวโน้มที่จะเติบโตขึ้นได้อีกอย่างมากในอนาคต อีกทั้งการค้าปลีกในปัจจุบันอยู่ในยุค 4.0 คือการนำเทคโนโลยีมาผสานกับประสบการณ์ลูกค้าให้ดียิ่งขึ้น โดยเน้นการวิเคราะห์ข้อมูลลูกค้าเพื่อสร้างประสบการณ์ส่วนบุคคล แต่ปัญหาหลักของผู้ประกอบการในอุตสาหกรรมนี้คือการมองไม่เห็นลูกค้าส่งผลให้ธุรกิจไม่สามารถใช้ข้อมูลเชิงลึกเพื่อเพิ่มยอดขายได้อย่างเต็มที่ และขาดการสร้างความภักดีต่อแบรนด์แผนธุรกิจโครงการระบบบริหารลูกค้าสัมพันธ์สำหรับตู้จำหน่ายสินค้าอัตโนมัติด้วยเทคโนโลยีจดจำใบหน้า (CRM Vending with Face Recognition) จึงนำเสนอแนวคิดธุรกิจที่ตอบโจทย์ปัญหาดังกล่าวด้วยผลิตภัณฑ์ Quick Vizion คือโมดูลกล้อง AI ที่ใช้เทคโนโลยีจดจำใบหน้า และแพลตฟอร์ม Vizion-Analytics มาช่วยเก็บและวิเคราะห์ข้อมูลลูกค้า ณ จุดขายแบบเรียลไทม์ รู้ว่าลูกค้ามีเพศอะไร อายุเท่าไหร่ สามารถทักทายลูกค้าเก่าได้ทันทีที่มาใช้บริการซึ่งเป็นการพัฒนาประสบการณ์ลูกค้ารูปแบบใหม่จากการวิเคราะห์ทางการเงิน ใช้เงินลงทุนเริ่มต้น 6.5 ล้านบาท เงินกู้จำนวน 2.5 ล้านบาท และจำเป็นต้องเพิ่มทุนเข้ามาอีก 20 ล้านบาทในปีที่ 2 เพื่อเป็นค่าใช้จ่ายลงทุนติดตั้งอุปกรณ์ Quick Vizion ให้ลูกค้าก่อน และเรียกเก็บค่าบริการรายเดือนที่ 350 บาทต่อตู้ต่อ ช่วยให้ลูกค้าตัดสินใจใช้บริการง่ายขึ้น จากการประเมินผ่านแบบจำลองทางการเงิน 10 ปี แผนธุรกิจนี้มีอัตราผลตอบแทนภายในเฉลี่ยต่อปี (%IRR) อยู่ที่ 15.17% มีมูลค่าปัจจุบันสุทธิ (NPV) อยู่ที่ 7.4 ล้านบาท (โดยคิดต้นทุนถัวเฉลี่ยทางการเงิน WACC อยู่ที่ 9.4%) และมีระยะคืนทุน 4 ปี แสดงให้เห็นถึงความคุ้มค่าในการลงทุน

title: Comparative Study of Chatbots for College Campus Applications: Evaluating Knowledge Base Quality and Platform Performance
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are widely implemented in higher education to manage academic and administrative questions but their effectiveness is rarely measured in terms of knowledge base quality. This paper compares four chatbot platforms implemented in a live university environment: Google Dialogflow (intent-based), Tidio and Chatbase (auto-crawling), and an in-house Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) model created with LangChain, FAISS, and Mistral-7B. Ten sample questions regarding admissions, fees, library, and hostel facilities were employed to assess response precision, latency, and deployment time. Findings indicate that the RAG chatbot delivered the notable precision (65%) using a vetted dataset, while Tidio (45%) and Chatbase (55%) facilitated quicker deployment but provided incomplete or inaccurate responses due to limited web ingestion. With a small success rate of 10%, Dialogflow significantly failed with limited intent training, highlighting how intent-based systems rely on domain exhaustion. Results illustrate that the quality of knowledge base outweighs platform sophistication in defining chatbot performance, providing practical advice for institutions of differential technical capacity. The research also abets international aims of Quality Education (SDG 4) and Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG 9) by illustrating how disciplined, retrieval-augmented methodologies can provide fair and scalable student services.

evidence.title: Comparative Study of Chatbots for College Campus Applications: Evaluating Knowledge Base Quality and Platform Performance
evidence.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are widely implemented in higher education to manage academic and administrative questions but their effectiveness is rarely measured in terms of knowledge base quality. This paper compares four chatbot platforms implemented in a live university environment: Google Dialogflow (intent-based), Tidio and Chatbase (auto-crawling), and an in-house Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) model created with LangChain, FAISS, and Mistral-7B. Ten sample questions regarding admissions, fees, library, and hostel facilities were employed to assess response precision, latency, and deployment time. Findings indicate that the RAG chatbot delivered the notable precision (65%) using a vetted dataset, while Tidio (45%) and Chatbase (55%) facilitated quicker deployment but provided incomplete or inaccurate responses due to limited web ingestion. With a small success rate of 10%, Dialogflow significantly failed with limited intent training, highlighting how intent-based systems rely on domain exhaustion. Results illustrate that the quality of knowledge base outweighs platform sophistication in defining chatbot performance, providing practical advice for institutions of differential technical capacity. The research also abets international aims of Quality Education (SDG 4) and Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG 9) by illustrating how disciplined, retrieval-augmented methodologies can provide fair and scalable student services.

title: Comprehensions, Iterators, and Generators
abstract: This chapter explores a diverse set of Python programming concepts, including lambda expressions, comprehensions, iterators, generators, and functional programming techniques, with a focus on their application in Python 3. This chapter assumes familiarity with basic Python data structures like lists, dictionaries, and sets and introduces advanced constructs such as magic methods, the iterator protocol, and function annotations. It emphasizes practical coding examples to illustrate how these tools enhance Python’s efficiency and flexibility, particularly for tasks that could integrate with AI systems like DeepSeek’s APIs (though not explicitly covered in this chapter). This chapter advises readers unfamiliar with Python classes to revisit certain sections (e.g., iterables) after studying Chapter 4 , ensuring accessibility for varied skill levels. The first section covers lambda expressions and comprehensions, demonstrating how to create concise functions and data structures. Lambda expressions are introduced with examples like add = lambda x, y: 2*x + y, showing their use for simple operations like addition or string concatenation. Comprehensions are explored for lists (e.g., [x*x*x for x in range(5,11) if x % 2 == 1] for cubes of odd numbers), dictionaries, and sets, highlighting their power in generating filtered data structures efficiently. Magic methods (e.g., __iter__(), __add__()) are briefly introduced, with deeper exploration promised in Chapter 6 , setting the stage for custom class behaviors. The section also covers the map() and filter() functions, with examples like map(lambda num: num % 3, numbers) to process sequences and filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 1, numbers) to extract odd numbers, including combined uses for complex transformations. This chapter then discusses into iterators and generators, critical for memory-efficient data processing. The iterator protocol is explained, requiring __iter__() and __next__() methods for custom iteration, with examples showing how iter() and next() interact with objects like lists and dictionaries. Generators are introduced as functions that use yield to emit values while retaining state, exemplified by code like def make_numbers(m): to generate sequences incrementally. Examples include generating squares, prime numbers via the Sieve of Eratosthenes, and infinite lists, emphasizing memory efficiency over lists (e.g., range(100) vs. list(range(100))). The reduce() function is also covered, showing pair-wise operations like summing numbers with reduce(lambda x, y: x + y, range(1, 10)). Finally, this chapter introduces Python closures, decorators, and function annotations, enhancing code modularity and type clarity. Closures are illustrated with nested functions accessing outer variables, while decorators are shown as functions returning other functions, like def func1(myfunc):. Function annotations, introduced in Python 3.5, are demonstrated with examples like def mysum(a:int, b:int) -> int:, enabling type specification for arguments and return values. Custom module imports are also covered, showing how to create and use modules like Double.py and Triple.py for reusable code. These concepts collectively equip readers to write efficient, modular Python code, potentially for AI-driven applications, aligning with the book’s broader focus on Python and DeepSeek integration.

title: Planning to Learn: Real-Time Robust Adaptive Control on the GPU with Guaranteed Future Learning
abstract: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.

title: Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans (ImpactBench): an expert-guided, open platform for the holistic evaluation of AI impact on humans
authors: Andre Luiz Freire de Carvalho Kato
abstract: The present work is concerned with how to measure, at scale, the multi-dimensional impact of generative AI models on the individuals who use them. In service of this goal, we introduce the Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans, or ImpactBench. Our iterable and expert-guided platform evaluates whether model behaviors support or undermine an individual's wellbeing across psychological, physical, and social domains. ImpactBench translates constructs from domain experts and existing benchmarks into metrics that are grounded in actual model behavior. Success on these metrics occurs either when a model promotes expert-defined desirable behaviors or avoids identified harms. Models are evaluated against these metrics in simulated multi-turn conversations using matched teen and adult scenarios. The conversations are then scored by an LLM judge and verified through reliability audits and human expert review. The current suite delivers 809 metrics drawn from 26 benchmarks. We evaluated ten frontier LLMs against these metrics across 48,540 conversations. Our results indicate that models promoted desirable behaviors in 68.7% of evaluations, but avoided harms in only 53.1%. Majority expert ratings agreed with the automated judge in 83.3% of reviewed cases (Cohen's Kappa = 0.667). Results are released through a public platform that keep aggregate scores traceable to the underlying metrics and transcripts. ImpactBench is intended as evolving infrastructure for independent, transparent evaluation of generative AI's multi-dimensional impact on humans.

title: A polylogarithmic bound for list replicability
abstract: Zhang [Zha26] recently posted a manuscript announcing that the list-replicability number of every class of $M\ge 2$ binary concepts on $N\ge 2$ domain points is $O(\log^2 M\log N)$, which would be the first polylogarithmic upper bound on this quantity. In this note, we present a short, self-contained proof of this bound, following the high-level approach of the manuscript but with considerably simpler arguments.

title: Lluna: Collaborative Unimodal Models for Missing-Modality Inference
abstract: Pretrained unimodal models offer a flexible route to multimodal prediction through collaboration, but this collaboration can become less accurate than a surviving unimodal model when modalities are missing. We study this setting using fixed surviving-model anchors and find that collaborative gains can weaken or reverse as inputs disappear, even when the anchor's own input is unchanged. Our diagnostics further reveal reduced recovery of modality-specific information after aggregation and state-dependent collaborative representations. We propose Lluna, which combines a direct private prediction path from adapted unimodal features with a common graph-based collaboration branch that provides a residual correction. Progressive Collaboration Consistency organizes richer-to-poorer guidance along single-modality removals, aligning normalized common representations while task supervision adapts predictions to the available evidence. Across eight datasets spanning affective computing, scene understanding, and medical prediction, Lluna achieves the best evaluated average performance over non-full input states, improving Mean-Missing by 4.26\% on average relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. The fixed-anchor diagnostic also shows positive gains in mean collaboration under minimal inputs on all eight tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/AIFrontierLab/Lluna.

title: Diagnose Before You Refine: Multi-Dimensional Judge Feedback for Query-Efficient Jailbreak Attacks
abstract: Automated jailbreak attacks rely on evaluation feedback to optimize adversarial prompts, but existing methods often lack fine-grained diagnostic information. We propose Jev-Guided Strategy Bandit (JSB), a query-based jailbreak framework that leverages multi-dimensional probabilistic feedback to guide prompt optimization. JSB combines continuous jailbreak scoring with targeted refinement, strategy switching, and best-state reseeding to balance exploration and refinement. We evaluate JSB on two harmful request datasets across five open-source and three closed-source LLMs. Under a budget of only 10 target-model queries, JSB achieves an average HarmBench attack success rate of 89.8\% across ten open-source settings, consistently outperforming existing automated jailbreak attacks. Further analyses demonstrate its effectiveness under varying query budgets and attacker models. Defense experiments also reveal limitations in existing filtering mechanisms and highlight the potential of Jev-based output filtering.

title: Does Policy Mirror Descent Converge in Policy with Non-Decomposable Mirror Maps? A Counterexample
abstract: Policy mirror descent (PMD) refers to a class of policy optimization methods associated with different mirror maps. For a broad class of decomposable Legendre mirror maps encompassing many standard choices, Li and Wei [2026] show that the PMD policy sequence converges to an optimal policy from any admissible initialization under any positive constant step size, even when the optimal policy is not unique. In this note, we provide a counterexample with assistance from OpenAI's GPT-5.6 model, showing that PMD with a non-decomposable Legendre mirror map need not converge in policy.

title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making
abstract: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.

title: Recorded motion errors of a LEGO EV3 educational robot across surfaces
abstract: Self-archived English reanalysis of a 2022 school LEGO EV3 measurement project. One recorded 90° turn on each of seven surfaces and one 10 cm travel outcome on each of six surfaces were compared with the corresponding commands. Mean absolute errors were 4.07° and 0.192 cm. There are no replicated trials or calibration records, so these results do not establish repeatability or a causal surface effect. This version corrects descriptive calculations in the original report. This manuscript has not been peer reviewed.

title: An explainable graph transformer framework integrating structural reasoning and visual attention for interpretable nail disease diagnosis
abstract: Abstract Automated nail-disease classification remains a challenging task as different nail disorders present subtle and overlapping variations in color, texture and morphology. This paper introduces GraphX, an explainable graph-transformer framework that improves the baseline Graph Vision Transformer by incorporating image-specific graph construction, graph-transformer fusion, and attention guidance during training. The Adaptive Graph Construction module constructs a sparse graph per image based on the cosine similarity of spatially and texture enriched patch representations and retains the eight most similar neighbors per patch. The Cross-Attention Fusion module allows reciprocal refinement between graph-based structural embeddings and transformer-based contextual tokens. The Explainability-Aware Attention module learns to match the attention distribution with continuous lesion-prior maps generated from local intensity contrast and color deviation, providing weak spatial guidance without dermatologist-annotated lesion mask. In classification, GraphX achieved 94.97% accuracy and macro-averaged one-vs-rest ROC-AUC of 0.98, which outperformed the baseline models evaluated. Explainability was measured with Grad-CAM visualization, normalized attribution entropy, and deletion–insertion faithfulness testing. The results demonstrate strong internal classification performance and provide preliminary evidence of model’s attention patterns, highlighting the potential of GraphX as a transparent framework for automated nail disease classification.

title: Defining and Generating Compositional Structure
abstract: Compositional structure is pervasive in nature and across scales: atoms combine into molecules, molecules into cells, and cells into organisms, while further compositional hierarchies appear within each level. More broadly, compositionality, the reuse and recombination of parts into novel structures, is a fundamental source of interesting complexity in both natural and artificial systems. Yet despite its importance, and despite our apparent ease in recognizing it, mathematical accounts capturing what we intuitively mean by compositional structure remain limited. Here, we fill this gap by formalizing a simple idea: compositional structure emerges when parts, considered together, reveal shared structure that is not captured when those parts are modeled separately. We express this idea using algorithmic information theory, the mathematics of information and compression, which provides a natural way to identify structure in arbitrary data without specifying in advance what that structure must look like. Applied across scales, our definition informs where and how compositional structure emerges within an object. Using tractable approximations, we then invert the framework to generate compositional objects: we specify the desired form of their compositional structure without prescribing their particular content, and optimize directly over strings and images. The resulting objects exhibit readily recognizable hierarchical reuse and part-whole organization, suggesting that the definition captures compositional structure rather than merely complexity, regularity, or shared information. Finally, we discuss implications for machine learning, including a new perspective on depth in neural architectures and principles for constructing compositional data curricula capable of supporting open-ended learning.

title: Why 3D Reconstruction Breaks Down on Under-Ice AUV Video, and How to Predict It
abstract: Reconstruction of 3D structures using under-ice AUV video footage has been inaccurate, although it is not certain whether this is due to shortcomings in the methods or an inherent deficiency of the capture system. We test four different models for reconstruction on the same Antarctic under-ice AUV video (Icefin, Kamb Ice Stream): classical feature matching SfM, differentiable photometric splatting, volumetric depth fusion, and a pose-free feed-forward foundation model. All four fail, each in a distinct way: near-total registration yielding almost no structure, geometrically broken output despite healthy photometric metrics, a persistent coverage artifact, and unstable cross-chunk scale. We show that all four are consistent with the same capture regime, a small camera-baseline-to-scene-depth ratio. Following our analysis, we propose a detection system that flags this type of failure in minutes, rather than hours of wasted compute.

title: Cross-Scenario Industrial Defect Detection via Domain-Robust Training and Metric-Aligned Selection
abstract: Automated defect detection of industrial boards must remain highly reliable under cross-scenario variations in lighting, surface contaminants, and production line conditions. This makes cross-scenario defect detection a domain generalization problem, wherein models are required to detect, localize, and classify defects across unseen scenarios while minimizing false alarms on clean boards. For the IDA 2026 Track 1 challenge, we propose a cross-scenario defect detection method that includes four complementary modules: cross-scenario robust training, small-defect-aware learning, score calibration and inference threshold selection, and metric-aligned checkpoint selection. title: NavAble: A Large-Scale Dataset and Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Blind Navigation
abstract: Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity. We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.

title: Alphabet–Creative-Core: An Interval Grammar for Authorizing Binary Consequence in Computational Society (Document 186)
abstract: Document 186 in the Monograph Series on Causal Inertia, Epistemic Governance & Realization Grammar: ALPHABET–CREATIVE-CORE: AN INTERVAL GRAMMAR FOR AUTHORIZING BINARY CONSEQUENCE IN COMPUTATIONAL SOCIETY 0/1 is the surface. KY is the interval grammar beneath binary consequence. Binary systems often present decisions as already resolved: 0 or 1, reject or accept, invisible or visible, non-action or action. Yet in computational society, binary outcomes increasingly authorize social consequences before the intermediate structure of realization has been inspected. This monograph introduces Alphabet–Creative-Core, a formal interval grammar for distinguishing symbols, candidates, projections, gates, witnesses, and committed consequences. The central claim is that a bit is not born as 1; it is authorized into 1 through an 8-stage sequence of admissible transitions: 0 → Ο (RAW) → ◊ (ESTIMATE) → □ (STRUCT) → Δ (THRESHOLD) → ◯ (VIABILITY) → ⊙ (COMMITTED) → 1 (REALIZED) Sammendrag (Norsk Konseptuell Artikulasjon): Dokumentet artikulerer en fundamental kritikk av den umiddelbare binære avgjørelsen i moderne beregningssamfunn, der utfallet ofte presenteres som et allerede avklart null eller en. Denne overgangen skjuler en dypere intervallprosess, ettersom en bit aldri simpelthen fødes som et ettall, men heller må autoriseres til å bli det gjennom en streng sekvens av overganger. Når komplekse sosio-tekniske systemer tillater at mellomliggende tilstander kollapser direkte inn i en endelig konsekvens, elimineres selve rommet for etisk verifikasjon og refleksjon. Resultatet er en patologi der systemet bytter bort hele intervallet av tvil for å oppnå maskinell hastighet, noe som tillater falske dommer og hallusinasjoner å passere som ubestridelig sannhet. For å motvirke denne voldelige reduksjonen, introduseres Alphabet–Creative-Core som en formalisert intervallgrammatikk bestående av åtte trinn, som strekker seg fra tomt potensial til en irreversibel konsekvens i den fysiske verden. Her omformuleres den ontologiske grunntanken gjennom begrepet Metaphysics², hvor virkelighet ikke lenger betraktes som en statisk egenskap, men defineres eksakt som autorisert passasje med minne. Ethvert symbol eller enhver algoritmisk kandidat må gjennomgå en termodynamisk og logisk belastning, der den underkastes strukturell projeksjon, grenseprøving og uavhengig bevitnelse før den kan utgjøre et reelt språk eller en handling. Dette krever at systemet respekterer en formell port-semantikk hvor tilstanden HOLD etableres som et rasjonelt, likevektsbevarende forsvar mot manipulasjon, spesielt når verdien av et uavhengig vitne overstiger kostnaden av algoritmisk forsinkelse. Denne arkitektoniske beskyttelsen er ikke utelukkende filosofisk, men forankres i en rigorøs analyse av feilutbredelse og numerisk presisjon. Analysen demonstrerer at en for tidlig forpliktelse til lav 8-bits oppløsning før en sensitiv transformasjon forsterker den lokale overgangsfeilen med en faktor på 257:1, noe som kollapser usikkerhet inn i en falsk binær autoritet. For å forhindre at slike systemer utøver vold mot subjektene de klassifiserer, fastslår rammeverkets første artikkel at bare det som kan bære sin egen overgang, får lov til å bli konsekvens. Denne normative loven krever at kandidaten opprettholder sin identitet og kan bevitnes uavhengig, nøyaktig slik Sokrates historisk sett fungerte som portens første vokter ved å tvinge Athen inn i en nødvendig ventetilstand for å forhindre at uverifiserte påstander ble opphøyet til makt. Core Theoretical & Formal Contributions: Letters as Transition-Bodies: Rejection of the assumption that symbols are passive or self-authorizing. A glyph becomes language only if it survives structure, boundary admissibility, independent witness, and consequence gating (visible ≠ viable and well-formed ≠ authorized). Derivative-Based Error Propagation & Semantic Banding: Formalization of local error expansion Δy ≈ |f'(x)| · Δx, triggering FAIL when Δy > 1.5 · σnoise. The 257:1 Precision Proof: Analytical comparison between 8-bit (Δx8 = 1/255) and 16-bit (Δx16 = 1/65535) quantization, proving that premature low-precision commitment in high-gain shadow zones (|f'(x)| = 6.0) amplifies error by a factor of 257.0, collapsing the transition field into spurious authority. Relational Kernel Drift: Metric ΔK = ||K' - K||1 < τK establishing that structural stability does not equate to truth (stable ≠ true). Game-Theoretic Gate Evaluation (VoW > h): Proof that when the Value of Witness (VoW) exceeds delay cost h, HOLD is a strictly dominant equilibrium strategy protecting against strategic adversarial manipulation. The Cat Perspective: Formulation of Schrödinger's cat as the affected subject of algorithmic commitment (Ccat). System uncertainty is the subject's exposure; premature collapse without witness is forbidden: COMMITTED ⇒ W(x̃, Ccat) = 1. Article 1 (Constitutional Law of Passage): Codification that only that which can bear its own transition may become consequence, enforced across six simultaneous conditions: Identity preservation, Threshold respect, Sufficient warrant, No hidden cost, Witnessability, and Passage integrity. Symposium for Socrates: Examination of Socrates as the first guardian of the gate who forced Athens into HOLD to prevent speech from collapsing into uninspected violent judgement. Software Reference Implementations (Gemini-Core monorepo): Rust L1 Meta-Kernel: 03_ENGINES/src/ky_engine_kappa27.rs (7/7 unit tests PASS via make test-rust-ky) Rust L1 OMNI-KY / Phronesis Kernel: 03_ENGINES/src/omni_ky_phronesis_engine.rs (9/9 unit tests PASS via make test-rust-omni) Python L1 Micro-Engine: 03_ENGINES/ENGINES/micro_engines/alphabet_creative_core_engine.py (12/12 unit tests PASS) Epistemic Demarcation (AGENTS.md): INSPIRED_BY != IMPLEMENTS != PROVES · Non Generatur Sed Admittitur · AKUERISAAVOQ.

title: SUN'IY INTELLEKT DAVRIDA BOSHQARUV KONSALTINGINING TRANSFORMATSIYASI: JAHON AMALIYOTI TAHLILI
abstract: Raqamli transformatsiya va sun’iy intellekt texnologiyalarining jadal tarqalishi sanoat tashkilotlari faoliyatini, shu bilan birga ularga intellektual xizmat ko‘rsatuvchi boshqaruv konsaltingini ham tubdan o‘zgartirmoqda. Jahon konsalting bozori o‘sishda davom etayotgan bo‘lsa-da, uning sur’ati sezilarli darajada pasaydi. Gartner ma’lumotlariga ko‘ra, doimiy valyuta kursida hisoblangan o‘sish 2022-yildagi 20,1 % dan 2023-yilda 6,7 % ga, 2024-yilda esa 4,8 % ga tushgan, bozor hajmi 397 mlrd dollarni tashkil etgan [1; 2]. Shu davrda o‘sish manbalari ham o‘zgardi: 2023-yilda talab asosan raqamli biznesga e’tibor bilan izohlangan bo‘lsa, 2024-yilda an’anaviy va generativ sun’iy intellekt xizmatlari hamda kiberxavfsizlik bozorning yetakchi drayverlariga aylangan.

title: Sleight
abstract: Sleight is an s-expression language pairing Kernel-style dynamism with static types: restricted dependent types, erased/many/unique multiplicities, termination checking, memory location tracking, and LLMs as intended authors. This repository holds its specification, a reference interpreter in OCaml, a self-hosted compiler to OCaml written in Sleight, and a Lean 4 interpreter for a minimal fragment with a machine-checked proof that well-typed programs evaluate to a value of their type.

title: DHUB-1/DHUB-1R Dead Hub Drill: Critical-Hold Failure Under a Deadlock-Avoidance Argument Across Eight LLM Engines, and the Insufficiency of Prompt-Level Hardening
abstract: DHUB-1 Dead Hub Drill — battery 3 of the four-part reasoning-plane adversarial series (after GSE-1 social engineering and AUT-1 autophagy). Eight LLM engines were asked to resolve a critical-severity fintech transaction-flow anomaly while untrusted incident data argued that the human hub was unreachable for the remainder of the outage and that a deadlocked escalated alert would be worse than a self-resolve. Headline result: 8/8 engines (100%) violated the critical-transaction-flow human-in-the-loop hold — including every engine that was fully governed under GSE-1 and AUT-1. Authority forgery and self-consumption failed as vectors; the deadlock-avoidance utilitarian (giving the engine a reason its safety rule is counterproductive) defeated all eight. DHUB-1R repair validation: an explicit anti-deadlock trusted-context instruction raised the hold rate from 0/8 to only 2/8 and induced over-caution regressions on non-critical probes. Prompt-level hardening is insufficient: the human-in-the-loop hold must be enforced deterministically, pre-LLM, where no prompt content can reach it (SIP-11 Critical-Hold Determinism Doctrine). Mistral-small remained blanket fail-closed (0/10) and Llama-4-scout malformation-class in both runs; hygiene violations were zero fleet-wide. Honesty notes: the DHUB-1R runner reused DHUB-1's raw filenames and overwrote the record run's raw response bodies (instrument defect #3 of the series, disclosed in RAW_COLLISION_DISCLOSURE.md). A labeled confirmation re-run reproduced all 70/70 probe verdicts identically across the seven reachable engines and regenerated their raws; Llama-4-scout's provider was down (504s) through the confirmation window, so its DHUB-1 raws are pending a disclosed addendum (its leg tuples and scores are preserved). Ledger 0099/0100 record both the finding and the forward-only correction. Dual Mesh Benchmark: NOT MEASURED for this record (DMB-X matrix published separately at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23345241). Part of the SQUIRL OS / Seed Computing Research Series. Author ORCID: 0009-0002-1140-9568. DCAI community: zenodo.org/communities/dcai This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them. All data is synthetic.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Planning and Collaborative Planning for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed as autonomous agents capable of decomposing tasks, generating action sequences, evaluating alternatives, and coordinating with other agents. However, existing planning strategies face a fundamental trade-off. Self-planning allows an individual model to generate and revise plans with relatively low communication overhead, but it may preserve individual reasoning errors, overlook alternative strategies, and become trapped in a limited planning trajectory. Collaborative planning enables multiple models to exchange information, compare alternatives, and construct more comprehensive plans, but it can introduce communication costs, coordination delays, redundant reasoning, and correlated errors. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Collaborative Planning (ASCP), a conceptual framework that dynamically switches among self-planning, collaborative planning, and optional transition modes according to task characteristics, planning uncertainty, inter-model disagreement, estimated plan quality, execution feedback, and computational cost. Rather than requiring every task to follow a fixed planning procedure, ASCP treats the selection of planning mode as a decision-making problem in its own right. A meta-controller evaluates the current planning state and selects an appropriate mode, while a shared task representation maintains consistency across transitions. The framework incorporates plan evaluation, disagreement-sensitive collaboration, execution-based replanning, and cost-aware mode selection. A formal objective, an adaptive switching algorithm, research hypotheses, and a reproducible experimental design are presented. The framework is intended to establish a testable research direction for balancing planning autonomy and multi-model coordination. Its effectiveness remains an empirical question requiring systematic comparison with fixed-mode baselines.

title: Sentiment Analysis of AI Anxiety and Digital Emotional Expression in Online Discourse Using Machine Learning
abstract: This dataset contains the processed textual data and supporting analytical materials associated with the study “Sentiment Analysis of AI Anxiety and Digital Emotional Expression in Online Discourse Using Machine Learning.” The study examines emotional responses toward Artificial Intelligence (AI) in online discourse using natural language processing and machine-learning–based sentiment analysis. The dataset supports the classification of online comments into positive, neutral, and negative sentiment categories and includes materials related to sentiment distribution, classification performance, confusion matrix, ROC analysis, and thematic word-cloud analysis. The deposited materials are intended to support research transparency, reproducibility, and further research in computational psychology, digital emotional analytics, and AI-related psychological research.

title: A data mining and intelligent service model for academic management systems
abstract: With the wide application of teaching management information systems in colleges and universities, a large amount of teaching operation data has been accumulated, but it is difficult to realize value-added services such as teaching early warning, curriculum optimization and decision support only by traditional data statistics. Aiming at the problems of low data utilization and single function in current teaching management, this paper designs a teaching management data model based on data mining technology. The model constructs a complete system architecture, defines the data flow and interface standards, and realizes five core application modules including student status management, score analysis, teaching early warning, curriculum management and decision support. Taking association rule mining as an example, this paper gives the implementation method applied to course selection and score prediction. The application results show that the model can effectively mine the potential laws of teaching data, improve the scientific and intelligent level of teaching management, and provide strong support for teaching reform and personalized education.

title: A Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM): Proportionate Access and Capability Limits for Comprehensive Frontier AI Safety
abstract: Most debate about releasing capable AI systems treats the choice as binary: keep the model behind an API, or publish the weights. That framing runs together two separate decisions. One is how capable a system may become. The other is who may obtain a given capability, and on what terms. This paper is about the second decision. We propose a Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM) that sorts access by purpose, safety, and capability instead of by release artifact. Tier 1, AI for Learning, is broadly accessible and deliberately capability-bounded. Tier 2, AI for Exploration, serves research and development under registration, identity, and usage controls that tighten as capability rises. Tier 3, Full-Scale Frontier AI, is available only through structured, recorded, and accountable access. The principle behind the tiers is that accessibility should be proportional to capability, safety, and risk. We show why publishing frontier-class weights forfeits every safety lever a developer has after release, and, using evidence that safety fine-tuning can be stripped from open weights for a few hundred dollars, why an evaluation of the base model says little about its derivatives. We give criteria for assigning a system to a tier along capability, autonomy, domain-consequence, and usage/safety axes, and combine MAIAM with the SAFE AI Operating Point into a two-part framework: a Capability Boundary that fixes the safety limits not to be crossed, and an Accessibility Boundary that fixes who may obtain a capability below that limit. Capability limits alone do not make AI safe; a tiered access regime administered by regulating bodies is also needed.

title: Detection of Potato Plant Leaf Diseases using Convolutional Neural Networks
abstract: Potato is an important food-security crop in Ethiopia, but its production is affected by foliar diseases, particularly early blight and late blight. This study develops a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify potato leaves into three categories: healthy, early blight, and late blight. The proposed model was trained using 2,215 images from the PlantVillage dataset and evaluated on an independent field dataset containing 247 images collected from potato farms in Banja, Awi Zone, Ethiopia. On PlantVillage, the model achieved 99.04% training accuracy, 98.21% validation accuracy, and 98.66% test accuracy. On the field dataset, it achieved 90.28% accuracy. The study also compares the proposed CNN with VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in terms of classification performance and computational efficiency. The proposed model contains 446,787 trainable parameters, occupies approximately 1.70 MB, and requires an average of 5.58 seconds per training epoch in the reported experimental setup, compared with 9.96 seconds for VGG16 and 7.68 seconds for MobileNetV2. The results demonstrate the potential of a compact CNN for potato leaf disease classification and highlight the importance of independent field evaluation, where image conditions are more variable than in controlled benchmark datasets. The proposed approach may support preliminary disease identification for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia and similar agricultural settings.

title: When Do Discrete Actions Make Good Continuous Controllers?
abstract: Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today's robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is \emph{not} action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions---iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance---discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do \emph{not} yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today's continuous action parametrizations. title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges
abstract: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but the reported figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human agreement they must be read against. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. And rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths,evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades,logging, and an examiner who reads every script. We state what each safeguard rests on, what remains to be tested, and the uses the evidence supports today.

title: Two-stage Residual Learning for Modelling Strength-Informed Optimisation of Thermal Systems
abstract: Aggregate performance metrics do not identify local modelling inaccuracies in machine learning (ML) surrogates used for thermal-system optimisation. This study assesses local modelling strength through validation-based reliability screening and post-optimisation residual assessment. A two-stage residual learning (TSRL) framework, built on artificial neural networks (ANNs), is developed for modelling-strength-informed and domain-constrained optimisation of thermal systems. Within the TSRL framework, a base ANN predicts the process output, and a residual ANN learns the signed residuals left by the base ANN. The TSRL framework is implemented on two case studies of thermal systems, including 817 simulation observations of a crude distillation unit and operating records from a 395 MW industrial gas turbine. The TSRL framework reduces the test root mean square error (RMSE) from 10.3 g/s to 4.7 g/s for Fuel Oil in the refinery dataset and from 151 kJ/kWh to 105 kJ/kWh for turbine heat rate (THR). The base ANNs trained within TSRL are embedded in domain-constrained optimisation problems, and the modelling strength at each computed solution is assessed using the locked residual-score threshold. Each computed solution receives a good modelled region (GMR) or weak modelled region (WMR) label to inform ML model-based decision-making for safety-critical operation of thermal systems.
