title: RIDI-REAL-UPDATES-v1: Individual correctness changes across released model updates and prediction from frozen fragility
abstract: Prospective, not yet executed. This study tests whether six pinned incumbent-to-successor language-model releases produce individual-question correctness changes even when aggregate benchmark performance is favourable, and whether the previously frozen RIDI-PREDICT-v1 fragility score F_B predicts those changes. The panel contains 800 questions (Natural Questions 250, HotpotQA 250, FEVER 300) with the byte-identical registered BM25 top-10 reference contexts from OSF xrzp5. No passage exchange will be performed. Twelve pinned instruction-tuned models will each run in main (single-question generation) and replay-floor (fixed batches of 16) conditions: 24 model-by-condition units. The optional API pair is excluded. Decoding, scoring, retries, blinding, model revisions and audit procedures are detailed in the attached protocol. A unit is retried only after a documented technical failure; no successful output or partial batch is reused. The full set of units must terminate before opening answers or performing scientific analysis. Prespecified endpoints and decisions: equal-benchmark-weight accuracy difference Delta, aggregate accept flags C0 and C1, per-question correctness disagreement D, per-model replay floors and excess E; H1 requires the 95% lower bound for E > 2 percentage points in at least four of six pairs and every C0-accepted pair; H2 tests pooled AUC of F_B with support at AUC >= .60 and 95% lower bound > .55; H3 tests an adjusted logistic association with specified covariates and prespecified separation/Firth handling, with odds-ratio lower bound > 1.3. The plan specifies 100,000 joint within-benchmark paired bootstrap resamples (seed 20261013). S1-S6 and independent auditing are also specified. Prior knowledge and limitations: P8 remains INCOMPLETE and is neither rerun nor rescued; RIDI-PREDICT's AUC results and a disclosed post-run analysis recovery are known. F_B values were known to the author; Qwen3-8B overlaps the predictors and is not an unseen model, and archived Qwen3 reference correctness is available for reproduction checks only. 'Accepted' is a prespecified study rule, not a claim about a vendor's actual release decision. No scientific generation in this new study has begun.

title: Python Using GPT-5 and Gemini
abstract: Python Using GPT‑5 and Gemini provides a practical, up‑to‑date guide that combines solid Python programming skills with real‑world integration of today’s leading large language models (LLMs). This book teaches essential Python techniques while showing readers exactly how to connect and use GPT‑5, Google Gemini, Claude, Grok, Perplexity, and other major 2026 models in their daily work. Readers will gain a strong foundation in Python data structures, comprehensions, generators, regular expressions, and object‑oriented programming. This book then moves into detailed coverage of GPT‑5 (including GPT‑5.4 and GPT‑5.3 Instant), Gemini 3.1, Claude Mythos, and Opus 4.6, along with practical Python code samples for chatbots, tool calling, data analysis, graphics generation, and integration with PowerPoint and Excel. Additional chapters explore LLM benchmarks, deceptive behaviors such as alignment faking and scheming, military AI applications, and comparisons between the major models, giving readers clear insight into their relative strengths and limitations. This book is written for intermediate Python developers, data scientists, technical professionals, and anyone who wants to move beyond basic prompting and build production‑ready applications that effectively combine Python with the latest generation of LLMs.

title: Web X.0 and intelligent automation beyond Web 3.0
abstract: This chapter examines the role of intelligent automation within the evolving paradigm of Web X.0, with particular emphasis on artificial intelligence (AI)-powered automation, machine learning, and predictive analytics. It analyzes how web-based user experiences are being enhanced through AI-driven personalized search engines, automated customer support services, and intelligent digital assistants. Furthermore, the chapter addresses ethical and socio-technical issues associated with these technologies, including algorithmic bias, data privacy and protection, and the implications for the future of work in an AI-intensive web ecosystem. Finally, the chapter evaluates interoperability and standardization aspects in relation to World Wide Web Consortium recommendations, decentralized identity frameworks, and mechanisms for cross-platform data compatibility.

title: Sign Betting for Misspecified Regression: Variance Adaptivity and Optimal Approximation
abstract: We study bounded regression under model misspecification, evaluating a function $f$ by its $L_1(P_X)$ distance to the conditional mean $η(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$, rather than the standard $L_2(P_X)$. This $L_1$ metric is natural for downstream decision problems such as bandits and reinforcement learning. We analyze the min--max estimator of Baraud & Maillard (2025), which we call \emph{sign-betting regression}. Our main results show that sign-betting regression achieves high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequalities under misspecification. Under realizability, our bound adapts to the average conditional variance and recovers the variance-adaptive rate of Li et al. (2026). We further characterize the optimal universal approximation factor for proper learning by showing that sign betting achieves factor 3, while no proper learner can satisfy a distribution-free, high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequality with a universal approximation factor strictly below 3. We extend the upper-bound analysis beyond finite classes and complement the theory with experiments in synthetic and real-world model-selection tasks.

title: Magnetic Susceptibility of Superconducting Films in the Meissner-London Regime
abstract: Extracting the London penetration depth, λ(T), from the measured magnetic susceptibility, χ(T), of a superconducting platelet in a perpendicular magnetic field requires knowing the function χ(λ) computed for the actual sample geometry. Thin films are increasingly important in quantum computing and superconducting electronics, most of which operate at ultra-low excitation fields in the vortex-free regime. Understanding their electromagnetic response in the Meissner--London (finite-λ, no vortices) state is therefore essential for extracting intrinsic properties such as the London penetration depth and superfluid phase stiffness. While numerous prior works have addressed different aspects of this problem, here we focus on providing an analytical semi-empirical representation of χ(λ) based on the 2D sheet-current model and establishing the limits of its applicability using two independent full 3D numerical solutions: finite-element modeling and a volume-current integral equation. As a result, we provide χ(λ) for a disc of radius a and thickness d in closed form, valid for all λ and for aspect ratios δequiv d/(2a)le0.05, and accurate to 0.1%. The two-dimensional sheet description with Pearl length Λ=2λ^2/d is adequate for δlesssim10^{-4} and λgtrsim 4d. Thicker films require the full closed form, which includes the three-dimensional corrections. Using the same numerical analysis, we provide an empirical formula that maps rectangular samples---the geometry most commonly used in experiments---onto a disc with an ``effective radius'' for subsequent calculation of χ(λ), and formulate a complete calibration protocol for whole-sample susceptibility measurements.

title: Object Pose from 2-D to 3-D Point and Line Correspondences
abstract: In this paper we present a method for optimally estimating the rotation and translation between a camera and a 3-D object from point and/or line correspondences. First we devise an error function and second we show how to minimize this error function. The quadratic nature of this function is made possible by representing rotation and translation with a dual number quaternion. We provide a detailed account of the computational aspects of a trust-region optimization method. This method compares favourably with Newton's method which has extensively been used to solve the problem at hand, with Faugeras-Toscani linear method [6] for calibrating a camera, and with the Levenberg-Marquardt non-linear optimization method. Finally we present some experimental results which demonstrate the robustness of our method with respect to image noise and matching errors.

title: Learning Optimal Classification Trees Robust to Distribution Shifts
abstract: We consider the problem of learning classification trees that are robust to distribution shifts between training and testing/deployment data. This problem arises frequently in high stakes settings such as public health and social work where data is often collected using self-reported surveys which are highly sensitive to e.g., the framing of the questions, the time when and place where the survey is conducted, and the level of comfort the interviewee has in sharing information with the interviewer. We propose a method for learning optimal robust classification trees based on mixed-integer robust optimization technology. In particular, we demonstrate that the problem of learning an optimal robust tree can be cast as a single-stage mixed-integer robust optimization problem with a highly nonlinear and discontinuous objective. We reformulate this problem equivalently as a two-stage linear robust optimization problem for which we devise a tailored solution procedure based on constraint generation. We evaluate the performance of our approach on numerous publicly available datasets, and compare the performance to a regularized, non-robust optimal tree. We show an increase of up to 12.48 percentage points in worst-case accuracy and of up to 4.85 percentage points in average-case accuracy across several datasets and distribution shifts from using our robust solution in comparison to the non-robust one.

title: Stochastic Risk Simulator: discrete-event multiagent simulation with bounded-memory PATL verification
abstract: Stochastic Risk Simulator is a general, domain-independent framework for evaluating risk in systems where many agents decide under uncertainty and against one another. It combines a discrete-event simulation of stochastic multiagent systems with exact strategic verification in probabilistic alternating-time temporal logic with bounded-memory, observation-based strategies (PATL_b). The framework follows the principle simulate to reach, solve to verify. The discrete-event engine executes a scenario and freezes the global state whenever an agent enters a state declared critical. From each snapshot, a bounded game between a coalition and its adversaries is solved exactly: branch probabilities are exact masses rather than samples, adversaries are unrestricted, and the coalition has imperfect information. Each risk question therefore returns a deterministic worst-case value, a verdict and the class of the strategy that attains it. Scenarios are specified entirely as JSON files validated against schemas (agents, environments, automata, distributions, events and coalition predicates); the engine contains no domain logic. Contents of this record- Source code of the simulation engine and the verifier (Python).- JSON schemas for scenario specification.- The case study of the accompanying article: liquidity runway of a startup with eight agent types, 111 agent instances, twenty-two automata and twelve predicates, in four macroeconomic regimes (Bull, Base, Bear, Crisis).- An automated test suite of 71 tests, including twenty-six games whose value is computed in closed form.- Documentation with the exact commands to reproduce the experiment of the article. The raw output (198,302 verifications) is not included; it is regenerated exactly from the configuration and the recorded seeds, and the documentation lists the number of verification rows expected in each regime. Accompanying articleKuzmanovski Reyes, B. Y., and Gavira Durón, N. Simulate to Reach, Solve to Verify: A General Risk Evaluation Framework via Multiagent Discrete-Event Simulation and Exact Strategic Verification. evidence.title: Stochastic Risk Simulator: discrete-event multiagent simulation with bounded-memory PATL verification
evidence.abstract: Stochastic Risk Simulator is a general, domain-independent framework for evaluating risk in systems where many agents decide under uncertainty and against one another. It combines a discrete-event simulation of stochastic multiagent systems with exact strategic verification in probabilistic alternating-time temporal logic with bounded-memory, observation-based strategies (PATL_b). The framework follows the principle simulate to reach, solve to verify. The discrete-event engine executes a scenario and freezes the global state whenever an agent enters a state declared critical. From each snapshot, a bounded game between a coalition and its adversaries is solved exactly: branch probabilities are exact masses rather than samples, adversaries are unrestricted, and the coalition has imperfect information. Each risk question therefore returns a deterministic worst-case value, a verdict and the class of the strategy that attains it. Scenarios are specified entirely as JSON files validated against schemas (agents, environments, automata, distributions, events and coalition predicates); the engine contains no domain logic. Contents of this record- Source code of the simulation engine and the verifier (Python).- JSON schemas for scenario specification.- The case study of the accompanying article: liquidity runway of a startup with eight agent types, 111 agent instances, twenty-two automata and twelve predicates, in four macroeconomic regimes (Bull, Base, Bear, Crisis).- An automated test suite of 71 tests, including twenty-six games whose value is computed in closed form.- Documentation with the exact commands to reproduce the experiment of the article. The raw output (198,302 verifications) is not included; it is regenerated exactly from the configuration and the recorded seeds, and the documentation lists the number of verification rows expected in each regime. title: FUZZYBOOST-HET: a competence-learned fuzzy-integral ensemble for stable feature selection
abstract: Replication bundle for FUZZYBOOST-HET, a feature selector that runs five heterogeneous selectors (XGBoost gain, random-forest impurity, mutual information, ANOVA F, RFE with random forest) over stratified bootstrap resamples of the training fold and aggregates their per-feature top-k membership profiles with a Choquet integral over a lambda-fuzzy measure whose densities are each selector's measured nested-cross-validation competence. Contents: fuzzyboost/ - the Python package (HET selector, FS/RFE companions, lambda-fuzzy measure, Sugeno and Choquet integrals, OWA, fuzzy TOPSIS, fuzzy c-means); scripts/ - every benchmark harness, the aggregation/competence/RFE ablations and the analysis layer that regenerates the reported statistics from the raw CSVs; data/ - a frozen mirror of 20 Penn Machine Learning Benchmarks (PMLB) datasets; results/ - raw per-cell result CSVs (20 datasets x 10 methods x 5 feature fractions) and the analysis outputs. Protocol: stratified 5-fold CV, random_state 42, selection strictly inside the training fold; balanced accuracy of a 100-tree class-balanced random forest; stability as mean pairwise Jaccard overlap between fold supports. Headline result over 96 paired cells: accuracy parity with XGBoost gain selection (+0.0043, Wilcoxon p = 0.342) with a significantly more stable support (+0.138 Jaccard, p = 8.5e-12). Five negative results are included, not suppressed. Install: pip install -r requirements.txt (Python 3.11+); full reproduction order in README.txt. Code: MIT; data and figures: CC BY 4.0.

title: Parallel-World Adaptive Routing for Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Adaptive Self-Routing, Collaborative Routing, and Cross-Model Coordination
abstract: Large language model (LLM) routing enables computational systems to select appropriate models, reasoning strategies, tools, or execution pathways for different inputs. Existing approaches have investigated adaptive model selection, cost-aware routing, model cascades, and multi-agent collaboration. However, a routing architecture that explicitly combines multiple parallel routing worlds derived from the same underlying model with heterogeneous external models, while adaptively switching between independent self-routing and collaborative routing, remains a promising direction for systematic investigation. This paper proposes Parallel-World Adaptive Routing (PWAR), a framework in which multiple routing worlds originate from the same base LLM but develop distinct routing policies, task preferences, exploration strategies, or decision criteria. Each world can independently select an execution pathway through adaptive self-routing or participate in collaborative routing with other worlds and heterogeneous external LLMs. A meta-routing controller determines when independent routing is sufficient, when cross-world coordination is beneficial, and when heterogeneous model collaboration is warranted. The framework incorporates task difficulty estimation, uncertainty assessment, resource constraints, routing-policy diversity, feedback-based adaptation, and outcome-aware coordination. Unlike a fixed routing architecture, PWAR treats the routing mode itself as an adaptive decision. It therefore distinguishes between selecting a destination and deciding how routing decisions should be produced. The paper formalizes the framework, presents its operational workflow and optimization objectives, and proposes an experimental protocol for evaluating effectiveness, computational cost, latency, robustness, and routing diversity. No experimental results are claimed in this conceptual paper. The proposed framework is intended to provide a testable research foundation for adaptive routing across parallel instances of a shared model and heterogeneous model ecosystems.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Parallel-World Self-Correction and Mutual Correction for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate incorrect, incomplete, or internally inconsistent responses. Self-correction allows a model to inspect and revise its own outputs, whereas mutual correction enables multiple model instances or heterogeneous models to identify and address one another's errors. However, relying exclusively on either mechanism may limit the diversity of corrective perspectives, increase computational costs, or reinforce existing mistakes. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Self-Correction and Mutual Correction (APSMC), a unified framework in which multiple LLMs dynamically switch between independent self-correction and collaborative mutual correction according to the observed characteristics of their outputs and the estimated benefits of further interaction. The framework introduces parallel worlds, defined as independently maintained corrective trajectories generated by the same underlying model under different correction objectives, prompts, reasoning constraints, or contextual perspectives. Each trajectory performs self-correction before selectively exchanging information with other trajectories. An adaptive controller determines whether the system should continue independent correction, initiate pairwise mutual correction, activate group-level correction, or terminate the process. The framework also supports heterogeneous LLMs that participate in correction without belonging to the same parallel-world group. Unlike fixed self-correction and permanently collaborative architectures, APSMC treats the choice between independent and collaborative correction as a dynamic decision-making problem. This paper formalizes the framework, presents a correction-selection algorithm, defines evaluation metrics, and proposes an experimental protocol for assessing accuracy, correction reliability, diversity, computational efficiency, and resistance to collective errors. The framework is a research proposal; its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing methods require systematic empirical validation.

title: Development and multi-database validation of machine learning models for 28-day mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and pulmonary hypertension
abstract: Background Early mortality prediction in critically ill patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) coexisting pulmonary hypertension (PH) remains challenging, particularly because prediction models developed in intensive care unit (ICU) database may not perform consistently across other healthcare systems. Methods This retrospective multicenter study employed two large-scale databases to establish and validate ML models for predicting early mortality in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The MIMIC-IV database served as the model-development cohort (2555 patients), with external validation conducted on eICU CRD (292 patients) database. Six ML algorithms were adopted: Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN). The baseline variables were screened to identify potential predictors via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) regression. Model interpretability was evaluated via SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis. Results The overall cohort consisted of 2,847 ICU patients with COPD and PH. Twelve consistently crucial clinical features were identified, including acute kidney injury, pneumonia, age, weight, heart rate, red blood cell distribution width (RDW), white blood cell (WBC), anion gap, chloride, creatinine, base excess, potential of hydrogen (pH). The Random Forest algorithm achieved the optimal performance, with a training Area Under Curve (AUC) of 0.938, internal validation AUC of 0.748, and eICU CRD external validation AUC of 0.800. SHAP analysis indicated that acute kidney injury was the most influential predictor, followed by base excess and RDW. Additionally, a web tool was developed in this study to facilitate the application of early death risk prediction in clinical practice. Conclusions This study is the multi-database validation of ML models for early mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The Random Forest model integrated with SHAP interpretability offers a reliable tool for clinical decision-making support, with consistent validity verified across two databases, including our internal validation cohort. This work provides a decision support tool to assist in identifying high-risk individuals within this complex comorbid population, and establishes a foundation for future studies with a more dynamic and personalized prognostic approach.

title: TGrasp6D: Task-Informed Vision-Language Priors and Pose Refinement enable Zero-Shot Task-Oriented 6DoF Grasping
abstract: Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation. Given the task of using a knife to "slice bread," a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for "hand[ing] the knife over," it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff. Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner. Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task- informed prior. This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%. We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects

title: Tulva: Practical Asynchronous Threshold FHE
abstract: We present Tulva, a practical threshold FHE scheme which equips a base FHE scheme with an asynchronous threshold decryption mechanism in a modular way. Our scheme simultaneously (1) is compatible with virtually any base FHE scheme and leaves its ciphertexts unchanged apart from an appended random tag, (2) supports a wide range of threshold profiles $(t,K)$ and ring degrees $\geq 256$ with 6-25 bits partial decryption per plaintext bit, and (3) achieves security in the presence of partial decryption queries on challenge ciphertexts based on the standard LWE assumption. We provide an open-source implementation, benchmark its threshold decryption performance and evaluate the end-to-end costs for typical privacy-preserving Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) use cases. For 16-out-of-512 threshold and a publicly preprocessed ciphertext, computing secret-dependent partial decryption and public share combination requires only 3.7 ms and 0.5 ms, respectively, on commodity hardware. Compared with the state-of-the-art synchronous scheme [Zyskind et al., CCS'25], we replace their ciphertext-independent yet interactive preparation of secret-correlated randomness with a public, ciphertext-dependent 0.5 s preprocessing step, eliminate interaction in the online phase while maintaining similar decryption time on the same machine, and support 32$\times$ more total users.

title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.

title: Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
abstract: We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.

title: HankelKANet: Lightweight Path Loss Estimation via Physics-Inspired Hankel Convolution
abstract: Accurate path loss (PL) estimation is essential for wireless network planning and optimization. This paper proposes HankelKANet, a lightweight physics-inspired network for PL estimation that structurally embeds electromagnetic propagation characteristics into the neural architecture. Built on a single residual UNet backbone, the proposed model integrates urban layout features with a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network(KAN). Specifically, the convolutional kernels are parameterized by the radial amplitudes of the zeroth- and first-order Hankel functions. This formulation acts as a physics-inspired nonlinear distance encoding, enabling the network to capture dominant attenuation characteristics directly without requiring additional physics-based loss terms. Experimental results demonstrate that HankelKANet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on both the simulated RadioMapSeer dataset and the real-world Huawei RSRPSet. Compared with the leading baseline, PEFNet, it reduces the parameter count by 78% and lowers the RMSE by 16.96% on the simulated data, while further exhibiting robust cross-dataset transferability and high data efficiency during target-domain adaptation. To interpret these empirical gains, we mathematically establish a parameter-conditional spatial gradient bound. Using discrete Dirichlet energy (DDE) and Jacobian sensitivity heatmaps, we empirically verify that this physical encoding intrinsically constrains the network's spatial derivatives. This structural smoothness effectively eliminates non-physical spatial ripples, preventing overfitting to simulator artifacts and serving as the fundamental driver for robust real world generalization.

title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate \textit{Active Generative Simulation}: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io

We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. title: Federated Distillation: A Survey
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing clients’ raw data, but parameter exchange can impose substantial communication costs and usually requires compatible model architectures. Federated distillation (FD) instead transfers predictive or intermediate knowledge through knowledge distillation (KD), which can support heterogeneous models and reduce communication in suitable settings. These benefits are not automatic: their magnitude depends on the transmitted knowledge, reference data, communication schedule, and threat model. This survey provides a challenge-centered synthesis of FD. We first formalize a representative public-data, response-based FD protocol and then organize existing methods by the FL challenges they address, including data, system, and model heterogeneity, client drift, catastrophic forgetting, communication cost, and privacy risk. We further review applications in industrial engineering, computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare, including recent federated adaptation of large language models. Finally, we identify five research priorities: richer transferred knowledge, joint treatment of interacting forms of heterogeneity, communication-aware distillation, threat-model-driven privacy protection, and standardized theory, benchmarks, and evaluation.

title: Consumer trust in ai-generated advertisement content
abstract: Diplomsko delo obravnava področje sodobnega oglaševanja s poudarkom na vplivu generativne umetne inteligence na zaupanje potrošnikov. Problem izhaja iz hitrega napredka tehnologij UI, ki podjetjem omogočajo avtomatizirano ustvarjanje naprednih oglasnih besedil, slik in videoposnetkov, medtem ko se pri potrošnikih pojavljajo skepticizem in etični pomisleki. Delo temelji na teoretični opredelitvi koncepta zaupanja in k temu sodečih pojmov, empirično pa analiziramo odziv slovenskih potrošnikov na konkretni UI-generiran video oglas z uporabo prilagojene merske lestvice ADTRUST. V raziskavi ugotavljamo zadržano in nevtralno splošno zaupanje potrošnikov v UI-generirane oglasne vsebine. Potrošniki najvišje ocenjujejo čustvene, estetske in tehnične vidike oglasov, bistveno nižje pa resničnost in pripravljenost za sprejemanje nakupnih odločitev na njihovi podlagi. Nadaljnji rezultati potrjujejo, da splošni pozitiven odnos do UI vpliva na višjo stopnjo zaupanja v UI-oglase, medtem ko demografske značilnosti, kot so spol, starost in izobrazba, ne pokažejo statistično pomembnih razlik v stopnji zaupanja.

title: Flatland: The Adventures of Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes
abstract: The training of neural networks often entails objective functions that are not globally L-smooth. For these functions, it is both theroetically and practically difficult to reply to the question: what is the largest possible step size that ensures the convergence of gradient descent (GD)? We address this longstanding open question in deep learning by providing a unifying definition of "large" step sizes that requires only local Lipschitz (or even Hölder) continuity of the gradient. We design first-order adaptive methods that provably yield large step sizes and show that they operate at the edge of stability (EoS) right from the start of the training. In particular, the loss decreases nonmonotonically and the product between the step size and sharpness, i.e., the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian, stays above the EoS threshold of 2 throughout training. Using our method, we are also able to minimize the sharpness all the way down to its global minimum. Contrary to expectation, we find that encountering globally-flat regions too early in the training may both slow down convergence and jeopardize the generalization ability of the network. Exploiting a self-stabilization argument, we allow GD to enter slightly sharper valleys and turn unsuccessful training runs into very successful ones.

title: Antigravity HFS: Memory-Resident Debian Kernel & Loopback Hole-Buffer Guard against Trailing Viruses
abstract: Release Version 1.0.0 of the HFS (Hole-buffer File System) autonomous architecture. Combines a memory-resident Debian 12/Linux 6.12+ kernel (toram), kernel RAM disk (/dev/ram0), loopback sparse container (hfs.img on /dev/loop0), and cryptographic SHA-256 hole-buffer and sector slack space hashing to detect and neutralize trailing viruses.

title: The Great Enterprise LLM Decoupling: Weight-Space IP Contagion, Orthogonal Backprop-Burn Infeasibility, Hardware-Enforced No-Learn Attestation, and Mandatory Third-Party Model Purge under Delaware Caremark Standards
abstract: Abstract: Global enterprise technology stacks—most notably Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) constituents and sovereign cloud operators—are executing an unprecedented structural purge of third-party frontier Large Language Models (LLMs), epitomized by the enterprise decoupling from external black-box providers ("Goodbye, Claude"). While superficially interpreted as cost optimization or routine vendor consolidation, this monograph proves that the decoupling is driven by an acute, existential legal and mathematical crisis: Weight-Space Intellectual Property (IP) Contagion and Fiduciary Liability Transmission. Building upon our forensic analysis of cross-border training data laundering (Project Panama, Record 23311531) and our Biological & Algorithmic IP Protection Covenants (NLL-v1.0-2026, Record 23358010), we establish four foundational results: (1) We formulate the Weight-Space Contagion Theorem, proving via non-diagonal Hessian cross-derivative coupling ($\nabla^2_{\theta} \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}$) that copyrighted works and sovereign trade secrets ingested during pre-training or fine-tuning cannot be surgically "unlearned" post-hoc without inducing catastrophic perplexity collapse (Orthogonal Backprop-Burn Infeasibility); (2) We model Transitive Enterprise Contamination, demonstrating how API outputs, synthetic distillation, and IDE code completions transmit copyright taint ($\phi_{\text{taint}} \to 100\%$) directly into proprietary corporate repositories; (3) We design a Hardware-Enforced Zero-Gradient Attestation Architecture ($\pi_{\text{no-learn}}$) utilizing Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and recursive STARK proofs over the 64-bit Goldilocks field ($\mathbb{F}_p, p = 2^{64} - 2^{32} + 1$) to guarantee mathematically that enterprise inference and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) execute with strictly zero weight updates ($\nabla_{\theta} W \equiv \mathbf{0}$); and (4) We prove under Delaware General Corporation Law (Caremark standard) and SEC Rule 15c3-5 / Item 1.05 disclosure mandates that corporate boards retaining un-auditable third-party LLMs after receiving constructive notice of supply-chain IP laundering face personal, non-exculpated liability for bad-faith breach of the duty of loyalty. Finally, we codify a 4-stage Enterprise Decoupling Protocol transitioning global infrastructure from contaminated black-box APIs to sovereign, clean-room verified in-house AI stacks.

title: Matched-Capacity Comparison of Additive and Multiplicative Neural Network Surrogates for Response Prediction of Steel Roof Trusses
authors: Dr. V. K. Verma Deepak Kulyal
abstract: ABSTRACT Repeated finite element analyses account for most of the computational effort in designing steel roof trusses, and neural network surrogates can remove much of this burden. However, the influence of the neuron model on surrogate quality is seldom examined under controlled conditions. In this work, an additive multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a multiplicative neuron model (MNM) of nearly equal size (211 and 196 trainable parameters, respectively) are compared. Training data were drawn from a parametric STAAD.Pro database of 46,140 Fink, Howe, Pratt and Warren trusses checked against IS 800:2007, in which non-compliant designs were deliberately retained. Using nineteen input variables, each network estimated eight continuous responses together with a binary pass/fail design status. On held-out test data, the mean coefficient of determination of the MLP ranged from 0.942 to 0.946 across the four profiles, compared with 0.700 to 0.775 for the MNM. The corresponding mean absolute percentage errors were 11–17 % and 26–37 %. Total weight was the most accurately estimated response (MLP R² ≥ 0.964), while the maximum utilisation ratio was the least accurate (R² ≈ 0.80–0.83), because the critical member shifts from one region of the design space to another. In pass/fail classification, the false negative rate of the MLP was 0.074–0.213, against 0.210–0.608 for the MNM. Since the MNM used a bounded geometric-mean aggregation and had marginally fewer parameters, its weaker performance is traced to the multiplicative form itself, which is poorly suited to the largely additive behaviour of truss responses. The MLP is therefore recommended as the surrogate, with its utilisation predictions regarded as the least reliable output. Key words: neural network surrogate, steel roof truss, multiplicative neuron model, multilayer perceptron, IS 800:2007, STAAD.Pro.

title: New PV output power forecasting approach using solar spectrum and deep learning for ultra-short time horizon
abstract: Accurate ultra-short-term forecasting of photovoltaic output is essential for improving the reliability and stability of solar energy systems. However, many existing forecasting methods rely primarily on irradiance-based features and do not fully exploit the information contained in the solar spectrum. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a two-stage approach to ultra-short-term forecasting of PV output current using solar spectral information. In the first stage, solar spectral irradiance is forecasted, while in the second stage, the PV array current is estimated to use the predicted spectra and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) regression model. The proposed method is compared with three alternative forecasting schemes. Firstly, a model based on statistical features of solar irradiance, including the moving-average clear-sky index (CSI ma ) and moving-average variance (σ ma ). Secondly, a model combining CSI ma , σ ma , irradiance, and spectral data. Thirdly, a model using irradiance, the white-to-total ratio ( wtr ), and sky images. Experiments were conducted using data collected in October 2025, and forecasting performance was evaluated for horizons of 1, 5, 10, 15, 30, and 60 minutes using R² score, MAE, MSE, and RMSE. The results show that forecasting accuracy decreases as the prediction horizon increases, with R² decreasing and error metrics increasing across all models. Nevertheless, the proposed spectral two-stage MLP-based approach achieves the best performance, with an R² of 0.971 for a 1-minute horizon and strong explanatory power (R² ≈ 0.87) for horizons up to 15 minutes. These results indicate that incorporating solar spectral information can significantly enhance the accuracy of ultra-short-term PV current forecasting.

title: Bayesian Learning to Select Fair Classifiers
abstract: Evaluations of classifiers (AI or human or agents) often assume a batch setting in which every agent produces labels on every example in a test set, which can be expensive or impractical in many contexts. This motivates online policies that adaptively select agents to query as examples arrive and update policies as outcomes are observed. We study the problem of selecting, in an online stream, the agent that best balances (i) predictive performance and (ii) subgroup fairness of a sensitive attribute, and that allows for delayed observations of true class labels. We formulate this as a Bayesian multi-armed bandit problem using Thompson Sampling, explicitly balancing accuracy and fairness. We conduct empirical evaluations on real-world datasets spanning problems involving tabular classifiers, large language models, and human labelers, demonstrating substantial reductions in regret relative to baselines. Our theoretical contributions include guarantees on the performance of the selected agent that incorporate both the accuracy and fairness aspects of the problem.

title: Universal enhancement of the pairing gap in a dilute Fermi superfluid
abstract: At zero temperature, a dilute Fermi gas with an attractive contact interaction forms a superfluid with gapped fermionic excitations. We show that the gap at weak coupling can be organized as a trans-series expansion in the interaction strength and the asymptotic Gor'kov-Melik-Barkhudarov gap. Low-energy virtual quasiparticles generate corrections that are linear in the gap with a leading coefficient nearly 25times larger than the other known coefficients. This substantially increases the gap at intermediate densities, highlighting that systematic corrections are crucial for quantitative predictions.

title: Controlling the latency in temporal coded spiking models for neuromorphic datasets
abstract: Exploiting temporal information in datasets with high temporal dependencies (such as spoken keyword recognition) by spiking models is still an open problem. Promising frameworks include Time-To-First coding (TTFS) and the inclusion of synaptic delays into learning. In TTFS, neurons are forced to spike at most once, forcing the network to found its learning on the spiking times of neurons rather than their spiking rate. Some models use the TTFS framework to directly compute the spiking time of Integrate-and-Fire (IF) or Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons. However, most models built in the TTFS framework have not been tested against datasets containing temporal information. Little is known about the latency of these models on temporal datasets, where the latency is the time taken by the network to correctly classify a sample. In this work, we study the behaviour of Delay Neural Networks (DeNN) models, i.e. models that directly compute the spiking time of neurons by bypassing the membrane potential and thresholding mechanisms of spiking neurons. We show how to analytically control their latency, and empirically study the latency-accuracy tradeoff in a dynamic temporal dataset.

title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
abstract: Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains 3.7-12.9x faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.

title: Statistical Inference in Reinforcement Learning: A Selective Survey
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is concerned with how intelligence agents take actions in a given environment to maximize the cumulative reward they receive. In healthcare, applying RL algorithms could assist patients in improving their health status. In ride-sharing platforms, applying RL algorithms could increase drivers’ income and customer satisfaction. For large language models, applying RL algorithms could align their outputs with human preferences. Over the past decade, RL has been arguably one of the most vibrant research frontiers in machine learning. Our goal is to highlight the value of statistical inference in RL for both the statistics and machine learning communities, and to promote the broader application of classical statistical inference tools in this vibrant area of research.

title: The use of artificial intelligence in the clothing industry
abstract: Diplomsko delo obravnava uporabo umetne inteligence v oblačilni industriji s poudarkom na personalizaciji uporabniške izkušnje. Predstavljene so rešitve, kot so priporočilni sistemi, predlogi velikosti, virtualno pomerjanje, personalizirano oglaševanje, napovedovanje trendov in upravljanje zalog. Rezultati anketne raziskave, v kateri je sodelovalo 140 oseb, so pokazali statistično značilno pozitivno povezanost med uporabo pripomočkov umetne inteligence in zaznano personalizacijo uporabniške izkušnje ter med zaznano personalizacijo in lojalnostjo potrošnikov. Ugotovljeno je bilo tudi, da imajo funkcije umetne inteligence pri nakupnem odločanju predvsem podporno, ne pa odločilne vloge. Učinkovitost umetne inteligence je tako odvisna predvsem od uporabnosti rešitev, kakovosti podatkov, transparentnosti njihove uporabe in zaupanja potrošnikov.
